ruststream-lapin is the RabbitMQ broker for RustStream, built on lapin, the AMQP 0.9.1 client. The guides take a RabbitMQ service from installation to production. Start with Getting started.
This section draws how RabbitMQ works, where ruststream-lapin sits between RabbitMQ and the RustStream runtime, and what that costs a service.
What ruststream-lapin costs on every message: throughput against the raw lapin client, and instructions and allocations of its code.

The first chart runs one scenario three ways on a real RabbitMQ node. Raw client drives lapin directly, by a loop written by hand. Broker crate is the same loop over this crate: the broker, the queue descriptor, the subscription stream, the delivery's own ack and its publisher, with no runtime around them. RustStream is the service a user writes, a #[subscriber] handler in an app, publishing through the same publisher. The first gap is what this crate costs over the client it wraps, and the second is what the runtime adds on top. Each loop is a bar from its best round to its slowest, with a dot at the best round and a notch at the median. The zero of the axis is the raw client's best round, and a dot right of zero is slower. A hollow dot is a loop whose difference from the raw client is smaller than the spread of the rounds. The table under the chart prints the best round with the median in parentheses. The two scenarios are the two queue types RabbitMQ ships. A classic queue holds its messages in memory and settles a delivery with a single frame. A quorum queue replicates every message through Raft and writes it down before it hands it out, and a transport that expensive leaves little room for anything above it to show.

The second chart counts what one message costs on the service's thread: instructions under callgrind and allocations under DHAT, in the steady state. Each scenario is a service on LapinBroker against the same node. The count includes the framework's dispatch, the codec, this crate's code and the work lapin does on that thread. lapin reads and writes the socket on a thread of its own, which is not counted. Most of a row's allocations are the client's: every acknowledgement and every publish creates promises and an internal task on the service's thread. Cold start is what connecting, opening the channels, declaring the queue, registering the consumer and taking the first delivery cost once.

How ruststream-lapin measures itself: the three loops, the run on a real node, the broker-bound arithmetic and the code count. The procedure is the framework's own (RustStream methodology), and this page states what it is on RabbitMQ.

One process runs each scenario three times over, as three loops that differ in one thing: what carries the messages. Raw client. lapin, driven directly by a loop written by hand: consume, decode, ack. Broker crate. This crate and nothing above it: the broker connects, the queue descriptor opens a subscription, and a loop pulls deliveries off its stream, decodes them and acks them. RustStream. The service a user writes: a #[subscriber] handler and the app around it. Everything else is equal across the three: the connection, the channel a subscription is given, the queue arguments, the prefetch window, the place of the ack, the decode into the same type, the payload bytes, the tokio runtime and the binary. The body is 512 bytes of JSON, published without asking for persistence. A classic queue keeps it in memory; a quorum queue has no other mode than its own replicated storage.

A fresh queue per run. Every run declares a queue of its own and deletes it afterwards, so no loop works through what the run before it left behind. The window opens at the first delivery and closes when the work on the last one is done, in all three loops. Every loop acknowledges a delivery after that point, so one acknowledgement out of the millions a run carries sits outside the number in each of them. The message count comes from a probe, which sets it so that every measured run lasts at least five seconds on any machine. The loops are interleaved: raw, crate, RustStream, three rounds. Each loop reports its best, median and worst round. A row is broker-bound when the raw client spent the run waiting on the server rather than working. That is arithmetic: a probe outside the rounds times one basic.qos the server answers, and the row is flagged when the round trips a delivery costs add up to at least half the time a message took. The round trip is published with the machine, so the arithmetic can be checked. An AMQP delivery waits for no round trip of its own, because the server pushes the body and answers no acknowledgement. What it waits for is the credit an acknowledgement returns, and the prefetch window spreads that wait over every message in it.

Each scenario of the cost chart is the service a user writes, on LapinBroker connected to the node of the compose stand, built without the testing feature. The service declares a classic queue at start, consumes it with the prefetch window of the comparison, and runs on a single-threaded tokio runtime. The queue is filled from another thread before the service handles anything, and the fill waits until the node has confirmed every message. Instructions come from callgrind and allocations from DHAT. A scenario runs over one delivery, then 1000, then 2000. The difference between the last two is the steady cost of a message, and the single delivery is the cold start. A real node answers in its own time, so how often the service's thread waits for the socket changes from run to run. Over seven runs of an unchanged tree a run's instructions moved by up to 2.4 percent, and its allocations by a block at most. A scenario's allocation floor sits a tenth of a percent above the highest count it produced, and just bench-code fails on an allocation above it. With --baseline=main the recipe also fails on more than five percent more instructions; a plain run applies no instruction limit. A failed run still prints the table, and under it every limit it breached, the old value beside the new one.

just bench The recipe starts the node from docker-compose.test.yml, runs both comparison scenarios, stops the node and rewrites docs/benchmarks/results.json. It takes a few minutes and wants the machine to itself. It clears RUSTFLAGS, so the binary is not tied to the CPU it was built on. Both recipes build the benchmarks the way a release is built, with fat link-time optimization across crates, so the numbers describe the code a service ships. just bench-code The code count takes under a minute and needs valgrind. The recipe installs the benchmark runner itself, at the release Cargo.lock pins. A number after the recipe's name sets the deliveries per measured run, as in just bench-code 2000; the published numbers are taken at the default of 1000. just bench-code --save-baseline=main on main records a baseline, and just bench-code --baseline=main on a branch compares with it.
What the benchmark numbers of ruststream-lapin measure, and what they do not allow you to conclude.

The three loops of a row are comparable with each other, because they ran in one process, interleaved, on one node. A row is not comparable with a row another broker crate publishes: the transports do different work per message. An overhead reported as indistinguishable is one where that loop and the raw client differ by less than the spread between runs of either. A figure below the run-to-run noise would read as precision that was never measured, so none is published. A broker-bound row is one where the raw client waited on the server for most of the run. The work of the crate and the runtime then happens inside that wait, and the difference comes out near zero. That is a lower bound on the cost, not a measurement of it.

documents.t: An instruction count holds this crate's code, the runtime above it and the work lapin does on the service's thread. The counts are absolute, the framework's own cost included; the core publishes that cost alone on its benchmarks page. The same count costs more time where it misses the cache, so a count is not a time. Every figure is the steady state, the difference between a run of 1000 deliveries and one of 2000. Connecting, opening the channels, declaring the queue and registering the consumer are the cold start, paid once.

A row is one consumer on one queue, a small body, and a node on the loopback. It measures what a delivery costs in this crate, not what RabbitMQ can carry. The prefetch window decides the absolute figures. A consumer that acknowledges every message and is allowed one unsettled delivery at a time spends a round trip per message, and all three loops come out at the speed of that round trip. The wide window these runs use is what lets the costs above the transport show at all, and moving it moves every column together. The numbers are a snapshot of one machine on one day, with the build recorded beside them. They are measured again by hand, on a machine given to the run alone: the differences they show are smaller than the noise of a shared one.

The runtime above it is the same for every broker. Everything RabbitMQ-specific is in this crate: the queue descriptors, the frames a settlement sends, where a retry goes, and the three publishing modes. One broker opens one connection. Each subscription consumes on a channel of its own, so its prefetch window and its errors stay its own. Fire-and-forget publishers share one channel. A confirms publisher, a transaction publisher and a requester each open a channel of their own on first use, because a confirm mode, a transaction and a reply consumer are channel state. A channel error closes one channel and leaves the connection up. A publisher's channel opens again on its next use, so one publish to a missing exchange does not stop the service publishing. LapinBroker declares nothing by default. A descriptor then states the topology the service expects, and a missing queue fails its subscription. declare_topology(true) makes each subscription declare its exchanges, its queue and its bindings, in that order. A requester reads its replies in a task on the runtime the broker connected on, whichever thread makes the first request. How the pieces start and stop is on Lifecycle, and the way of one delivery on Path.

Without workers, one loop runs the handler for each delivery in turn, so the queue's order holds and nothing runs side by side. The prefetch window decides how many deliveries wait in the service meanwhile. workers(n, by_key) runs n lanes. A delivery goes to the lane its key hashes to, and a lane runs its deliveries in order. The key is the amqp-partition-key header, which the producer sets. AMQP does not read it: it is a convention between the producer and this crate. A delivery without the header has no key, and such deliveries rotate over the lanes. Lanes need a window wider than one. With a prefetch of 1 the queue pushes the next delivery only after the last one settles, and the lanes take turns. The order a lane keeps is the order inside one consumer. Two instances of the service on one queue are two competing consumers, and the queue spreads the deliveries of one key over both. RabbitMQ's single active consumer (x-single-active-consumer), a queue argument set with argument, lets one consumer read the queue at a time. The consistent-hash exchange moves the same idea to the server. It spreads the routing keys over several queues, and each queue gets a subscription of its own. One key goes to one queue in normal operation, so its order holds across instances while each queue has one consumer. A batch handler takes what the queue has already pushed, up to the size the mount site names, so a batch is often smaller than that size.

The runtime connects the broker when the app starts. Connect opens the AMQP connection to the URI, with the connection_name the management UI shows, and opens the shared publish channel. A server that refuses the connection fails the start. Each subscription's descriptor resolves once, against the connected broker, and the start fails on the first one that cannot open: A quorum queue checks its retry declaration. max_attempts and dead_letter become the queue's own arguments, so they need each other and a broker that declares the queue. The subscription opens its channel. Under declare_topology(true) it declares its exchanges, its queue, its bindings and its delay target. A declaration that differs from what the server holds is refused with PRECONDITION_FAILED. It sends basic.qos with its prefetch window, when one is set. A delay the broker does not declare is checked to exist: its waiting queue or its delayed exchange. A missing one fails the start and names both the subscription and the target. It starts its consumer with basic.consume. A queue that does not exist fails here. The delay check exists because the delayed copy is published without waiting for an answer, and the original is acknowledged after it. The server drops a copy sent to a waiting queue that does not exist, so without the check the message would be lost with no error. It costs one round trip at startup and nothing per message. A service that only consumes opens no further channel. The first publish through a confirms or transaction policy, and the first request, open the channel each of them needs. Shutdown marks the connection closed first, so a publisher that still holds it cannot slip a message in, and then closes the connection with the AMQP close handshake. The server requeues whatever the subscriptions held unsettled. ClosedLapinBroker::handshake reports whether the handshake ran. A publisher or a requester that outlives the connection answers AmqpError::Closed after shutdown, and a delivery settled after shutdown reports an error instead of a settlement that never happened.

Recovery is disabled by default. With LapinBroker::auto_recover(true), the connected broker can be connected or reconnecting without changing its Rust type. is_connected() reports the AMQP connection state; channel and topology restoration may still be running when it returns true. Lapin restores the existing channels and their topology instead of rebuilding the application. Startup hooks are not rerun. recovery_retries(n) limits retries for startup and later recovery (16 by default). Exhaustion ends a consumer with a terminal consume error. Shutdown during recovery marks handles closed and wakes waiting consumers immediately; a later reconnected socket is closed in the background.

RabbitMQ routes a message through an exchange into queues by bindings, and a consumer reads one queue over a channel of a connection. It publishes to an exchange and gives the message a routing key. The exchange compares the message with its bindings, and every queue whose binding matches gets a copy. A message that matches no binding reaches no queue. A queue is storage that a consumer empties. A message leaves the queue once its consumer acknowledges it. Until then the server keeps it, and a delivery the consumer gives back or never settles returns to the queue. Every server has a default exchange with an empty name. Each queue is bound to it under its own name, so a publish to the default exchange with the routing key orders lands in the queue orders. That is how a service with no topology of its own still publishes to a queue. Exchanges, queues and bindings live in a virtual host, which the connection URI names. A client opens one TCP connection and runs its work on channels inside it. A channel is a light session with state of its own: a prefetch window, a confirm mode, a transaction. An error on a channel closes that channel and leaves the connection up. The model is AMQP 0.9.1 as RabbitMQ implements it (AMQP concepts, channels, the default exchange). How each exchange type routes is on Exchange types, how a queue pushes to its consumers on Consumers and prefetch, and how the two queue types differ on Classic and quorum queues.

A queue pushes deliveries to its consumers, each within a window of unacknowledged deliveries that its acknowledgements reopen. A queue pushes deliveries to two consumers, each with a prefetch window of two; an ack frees a slot, and a closed channel returns its deliveriesbasic.deliverbasic.deliverQueue ordersmessages wait in orderConsumer 1prefetch 2:2 unacknowledgedConsumer 2prefetch 2:2 unacknowledgedbasic.ack freesa slot, and the nextdelivery is pushedChannel closed:its unacknowledgeddeliveries return,marked redeliveredThe queue spreads deliveries over its consumers in turn,skipping a consumer whose window is full The diagram as text Queue orders messages wait in order → Consumer 1 prefetch 2: 2 unacknowledged: basic.deliver Queue orders messages wait in order → Consumer 2 prefetch 2: 2 unacknowledged: basic.deliver Consumer 1 prefetch 2: 2 unacknowledged → basic.ack frees a slot, and the next delivery is pushed Consumer 2 prefetch 2: 2 unacknowledged → Channel closed: its unacknowledged deliveries return, marked redelivered The queue spreads deliveries over its consumers in turn, skipping a consumer whose window is full A consumer does not ask for messages. It registers with basic.consume, and the queue pushes basic.deliver frames to it. Several consumers on one queue compete: the queue gives each message to one of them, in turn. The prefetch window is the number of deliveries a consumer may hold unacknowledged. Once the window is full, the queue pushes nothing more to that consumer until an acknowledgement frees a slot. This is how a slow handler slows the queue down instead of filling the service's memory. RabbitMQ sets the window with basic.qos, per consumer, and reads 0 as no limit. A delivery stays the consumer's until it is settled. basic.ack removes the message from the queue. basic.reject with requeue puts it back, and without requeue the queue drops it or dead-letters it. When a channel closes with deliveries still unsettled, the queue takes them back and delivers them again with the redelivered flag set.

Each subscription opens a channel of its own and one consumer on it. Before the consumer starts, the subscription sends basic.qos with its window: RabbitQueue::prefetch for one queue, or LapinBroker::prefetch for every subscription that sets none. The setting is a non-zero number, so a subscription that sets neither sends no basic.qos and runs with no limit. The window also bounds a batch. AMQP has no batch frame, so a batch handler's batch is collected on the client from what the queue has already pushed: up to the size the mount site names, or what arrived within batch_wait (50 milliseconds by default). A window smaller than the batch size caps the batch at the window. A dropped subscription closes its channel, and RabbitMQ requeues what it held unsettled. How the runtime settles each delivery is on Settlement and retries. The protocol rules are RabbitMQ's (consumer prefetch, consumer acknowledgements, work queues).

With connection recovery enabled, Lapin restores the consumer's existing channel, declared exchanges, queues and bindings, and reapplies its prefetch before resuming delivery. The stream waits through recoverable disconnects and ends with a consume error if retries run out. With recovery disabled, it follows the plain Lapin consumer's terminal behavior. Unsettled deliveries from queues that survive the disconnect can be redelivered. An old acknowledgement can fail after reconnect; the handler must tolerate processing a delivery again. Failed publishes are not replayed, and outstanding RPC deadlines keep running.

A publish to RabbitMQ ends when the frame is written, when the server confirms it, or when a channel transaction commits. Three ways a publish ends: fire-and-forget when the frame is written, confirms when the server answers, a transaction at the commitFire and forgetConfirmsTransactionbasic.publishReturns oncethe frame iswrittenconfirm.selectoncebasic.publishbasic.ack orbasic.nack foreach messagetx.selectoncebasic.publishone or moretx.commitcommit-ok:every publishvisibleA message no queue takes is confirmed and dropped:the crate publishes without the mandatory flag The diagram as text Fire and forget: basic.publish; Returns once the frame is written Confirms: confirm.select once; basic.publish; basic.ack or basic.nack for each message; A message no queue takes is confirmed and dropped: the crate publishes without the mandatory flag Transaction: tx.select once; basic.publish one or more; tx.commit; commit-ok: every publish visible basic.publish → Returns once the frame is written confirm.select once → basic.publish basic.publish → basic.ack or basic.nack for each message tx.select once → basic.publish one or more basic.publish one or more → tx.commit tx.commit → commit-ok: every publish visible basic.publish has no answer of its own. A publisher that sends it and moves on learns nothing about the message: a missing exchange or a queue that fails goes unseen. Publisher confirms add the answer. After confirm.select the channel numbers its publishes, and the server answers each one with basic.ack once it has taken responsibility for it. For a persistent message in a durable queue that means written to disk; for a quorum queue it means accepted by a quorum of replicas. basic.nack says the server could not handle the message, and it is rare: it comes from an internal error of a queue. A message that matches no binding is confirmed too. The exchange finds no queue, the server confirms the message and drops it. Only the mandatory flag makes the server return such a message to the publisher. A channel transaction stages publishes on the server. After tx.select, publishes wait until tx.commit; commit-ok says every one of them is visible, and tx.rollback discards them. Each commit is a round trip that waits for the server. RabbitMQ does not promise atomicity when a node fails during the commit.

The publish policy decides the mode, and a stronger mode is a different policy: Policy Channel A publish returns LapinPublish one channel shared by every such publisher of the connection once the frame is written ConfirmsPublish its own, in confirm mode once the server confirms; a negative confirm is an error ServerTxPublish its own, in transaction mode inside a transaction, at the commit A confirms or transaction channel opens on the first publish, so a policy that never publishes holds no channel. Every publish goes out without mandatory, so a confirmed publish can still have reached no queue: a confirm says the server took the message, not that a queue holds it. Messages are persistent unless the policy says otherwise. A channel error closes the channel and leaves the connection up. A fire-and-forget publish to an exchange that does not exist is enough, and the publisher does not see the server's answer. The next publish opens a new channel. A transaction channel that dies with a transaction open is the exception: the transaction lived on it, so the commit fails instead of reporting success. The transaction of ConfirmsPublish is a buffer in the service. The commit publishes the buffered messages in order and waits for every confirm. It is durable per message and not atomic: messages sent before a failed one stay published. The transaction of ServerTxPublish is RabbitMQ's own. It is one per channel, because tx.select puts the channel itself in transaction mode. The protocol rules are RabbitMQ's (publisher confirms, transactions).

A classic queue lives on one node and counts nothing; a quorum queue is replicated, counts failed deliveries and moves a spent message itself. Classic and quorum queues side by side: where each keeps its messages, what a requeue does, and what ends a message that keeps coming backlimit passedClassic queueQuorum queueOne nodeholds the messagesreject with requeue:back in the queue,nothing countedreject withoutrequeue: dead-lettered or droppedA leader and itsfollowers, by Raftreject with requeue:back in the queue,x-delivery-count + 1Past the deliverylimit: dead-lettered or droppedSince RabbitMQ 4.0 a quorum queue's delivery limitis 20 unless the queue sets another The diagram as text Classic queue: One node holds the messages; reject with requeue: back in the queue, nothing counted; reject without requeue: dead- lettered or dropped Quorum queue: A leader and its followers, by Raft; reject with requeue: back in the queue, x-delivery-count + 1; Past the delivery limit: dead- lettered or dropped reject with requeue: back in the queue, x-delivery-count + 1 → Past the delivery limit: dead- lettered or dropped: limit passed Since RabbitMQ 4.0 a quorum queue's delivery limit is 20 unless the queue sets another The type is fixed when the queue is declared, through the x-queue-type argument. Both types take the same consumers and the same settlement frames. They differ in where the messages live and in what a requeue costs a message. In RabbitMQ 4 a classic queue keeps its messages on one node, unreplicated. A rejected delivery with requeue goes back and can come round again without end. The queue keeps no count: a redelivery carries only the redelivered flag. A quorum queue replicates its messages over several nodes with the Raft protocol, and a quorum of them accepts each write. It is durable by definition. It counts the failed deliveries of each message and stamps the count on a redelivery as the x-delivery-count header. A message whose count passes the queue's delivery limit leaves the queue. Since RabbitMQ 4.0 the limit is 20 when the queue sets none. Since RabbitMQ 4.3 not every return counts. basic.reject and a channel that closes with the delivery unsettled count. basic.nack with requeue returns the message without counting it. A message that leaves a queue by a rejection without requeue, or past the delivery limit, goes to the queue's dead-letter exchange when it has one (x-dead-letter-exchange, with an optional x-dead-letter-routing-key). A queue with none drops it.

The queue type is a descriptor type, because it decides what a retry does: RabbitQueue for a classic queue and RabbitQuorumQueue for a quorum one. A quorum queue descriptor has no durable, exclusive or auto_delete step, since a quorum queue is always durable and shared. The crate settles a negative outcome with basic.reject, never with basic.nack. On one delivery the two frames do the same thing, and only the rejection counts on a quorum queue. A handler's retry() therefore spends one of the message's deliveries, and the queue's limit ends a message that keeps failing. Settlement and retries draws how each type answers a retry. The queue rules are RabbitMQ's (classic queues, quorum queues, poison message handling, dead letter exchanges).

LapinRequester opens a channel of its own on the first request, starts the reply consumer on it, and publishes every request on that channel. Each request carries a generated correlation-id, and the reply with the same id resolves the call. One task per requester reads the replies, on the runtime the broker connected on. Each exchange type reads a different part of a message to pick its queues: the routing key, a pattern over it, nothing, or the headers. The default exchange is a direct exchange, with every queue bound under its own name. A topic exchange reads the routing key as words separated by dots. A binding is a pattern over those words: * stands for exactly one word and # for zero or more. The key order.eu.placed matches order.*.placed and order.#, and does not match order.*. A fanout exchange ignores the key and copies the message into every queue bound to it. A headers exchange ignores the key too. It compares the message's headers with the binding's arguments. With x-match set to all every argument has to match, with any one is enough. In this crate a binding with arguments is bind_with. A message can match several bindings. It then reaches every matching queue, once per queue. The consistent-hash exchange comes from a plugin that ships with RabbitMQ and has to be enabled. It hashes the routing key and sends the message to one bound queue. A binding's key is its weight: a queue bound with weight 2 gets about twice the keys of a queue bound with weight 1. Messages with one routing key go to one queue in normal operation; a node restart can move a key to another queue. The crate offers it as RabbitExchange::consistent_hash under the plugin-consistent-hash feature, and Lanes and order compares it with lanes inside one subscription. RabbitExchange names the exchange of a binding. custom names any other type a plugin adds. The routing rules are RabbitMQ's (exchanges, topic exchanges, consistent hash exchange).

On one delivery it does what basic.reject does, and since RabbitMQ 4.3 only the rejection counts toward a quorum queue's delivery limit. A batch handler's outcome settles each delivery of the batch with the same frame. A reply that arrives through a requester needs no settlement: it comes to a consumer without acknowledgements.

The first delivery counts as one attempt. Who counts depends on the queue type. A classic queue counts nothing, so the runtime does. On a retry below the cap it rejects the original without requeue and publishes a copy to the default exchange under the queue's name, which lands at the back of the same queue. The copy carries the attempt number in the x-ruststream-retry-count header. At the cap the copy goes to the queue named by dead_letter instead, or, with no dead_letter, the delivery is rejected and nothing is published. On a classic queue that has a dead-letter exchange of its own, the rejection of each original reaches that exchange too. A quorum queue counts its deliveries itself. The pair becomes the queue's x-delivery-limit (max_attempts minus one, since the server counts returns) and its dead-letter route to the dead_letter queue. A retry is a plain basic.reject with requeue, and the server dead-letters the message once it passes the limit, whether the service is running or not. The arguments reach the queue only when this service declares it, so the pair needs declare_topology(true), and the start fails without it. A quorum queue publishes no copies, so a retry publisher (out_retry) does not compile on it.

AMQP has no delay per message, so the wait happens in one of three places. With no delay on a classic queue, the runtime holds the copy. It rejects the original and publishes the copy when a timer in the service fires. A graceful shutdown waits for the timer, and a process that dies before it fires loses the copy. On a quorum queue without delay the runtime has no copy to hold: the delivery is requeued at once, and a warning says the delay was dropped. Delay::dlx_ttl keeps the copy on the broker. The crate publishes it to a waiting queue, <queue>.retry by default, with the delay as its per-message expiration, and acknowledges the original after it on the same channel. When the expiration passes, the waiting queue dead-letters the copy back to the origin queue. A queue releases expired messages only from its head, so a short delay behind a long one waits for the long one; one waiting queue per delay keeps them apart. Delay::plugin_dme, under the plugin-dme feature, publishes the copy to an exchange of the delayed-message plugin, <queue>.delay by default, with the delay in its x-delay header. The plugin routes it to the origin queue once the delay has passed, and delays of different lengths do not wait for each other. Either target is infrastructure. Under declare_topology(true) each subscription declares its own. Without declaration the subscription checks at startup that the target exists, and a missing one fails the start, because the server would drop a copy sent to a waiting queue that does not exist. The copy is a new message, so the server counts it from zero. It carries the x-ruststream-retry-count header raised by one, and on a classic queue the runtime reads the cap from it before the copy is sent: a delivery at the cap goes to the dead-letter queue instead of waiting again. The rules on the server side are RabbitMQ's (negative acknowledgements, quorum queue delivery limit, dead lettering, per-message TTL, delayed message exchange).

The parts of ruststream-lapin a RabbitMQ service uses, one page per component: the broker (LapinBroker), its queue descriptors, its publish policies and the in-process transport a TestApp test runs on.

With the asyncapi feature the generated document speaks AMQP 0.9.1: the server, the queue behind each channel and the properties of each send. The core builds the AsyncAPI document from the app, before anything connects. This crate adds the specification's amqp binding, version 0.3.0, to the parts it knows about. The server reports the host and the AMQP version. A channel reports the queue behind a subscription, or the exchange a publish leaves through. An operation reports how a receive settles and which properties a send carries. The exchanges a queue is bound to ride the crate's own extension, x-ruststream-amqp. Everything comes from the service's own declarations: the broker, the queue descriptors and the publish policies. The document is published and shared, so no binding carries a credential. The binary #[ruststream::app] writes prints the document with asyncapi gen.

The dependency line: ruststream-lapin = { version = "0.7", features = ["asyncapi"] } The service registers its broker under the label rabbit, the key of its server in the document. cargo run --example lapin_asyncapi --features asyncapi -- asyncapi gen prints the document. A subscription's channel is its queue with durability and exclusivity; a publish names a routing key on an exchange, or a queue. A subscription's channel binding is is: queue. Its queue object carries the name and the durable, exclusive and autoDelete settings of the RabbitQueue descriptor. A channel the service publishes to is described from its publish policy. Its name is the destination the mount site resolved: a reply's name, the name of a slot entry, or a dead_letter(..) declaration. On a policy with a named exchange, the name is the routing key: the binding is is: routingKey with the exchange's name. On the default exchange the routing key is the queue a message lands in: the binding is is: queue with that queue's name. A queue's settings belong to the side that declares it, so this binding carries the name alone. A reply under DirectReplyTo goes to the address each request carries. Its channel therefore has no address, and the receive operation names the header the address is read from.

The channel inventory.check reports a transient, exclusive, auto-delete queue. The reply channel inventory.unrouted reports the exchange answers, and the dead-letter channel inventory.dead reports the queue of that name. Macros Manual examples/lapin_asyncapi.rs #[subscriber( RabbitQueue::new("inventory.check").durable(false).exclusive(true).auto_delete(true), reply("inventory.unrouted") )] async fn check(ask: &Ask) -> Stock { Stock { available: !ask.sku.is_empty(), } } fn service(broker: LapinBroker) -> RustStream { let inventory = AppInfo::new("inventory", "1.0.0"); RustStream::new(inventory).with_broker_labeled("rabbit", broker, |b| { b.include(check) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("inventory.dead") .out_reply(Publish::default().exchange("answers")) .transform(DirectReplyTo); b.include(on_event) .out( Restocks, Publish::default() .priority(4) .expiration(Duration::from_secs(30)), ) .build(); }) } examples/manual/lapin_asyncapi.rs /// A queue that lives as long as this service's connection. fn checks() -> RabbitQueue { RabbitQueue::new("inventory.check") .durable(false) .exclusive(true) .auto_delete(true) } fn service(broker: LapinBroker) -> RustStream { let inventory = AppInfo::new("inventory", "1.0.0"); RustStream::new(inventory).with_broker_labeled("rabbit", broker, |b| { let check = subscriber(checks(), Check).reply().to("inventory.unrouted"); b.include(check.build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("inventory.dead") .out_reply(Publish::default().exchange("answers")) .transform(DirectReplyTo); b.include(subscriber(events(), OnEvent).build()) .out( Restocks, Publish::default() .priority(4) .expiration(Duration::from_secs(30)), ) .build(); }) }

The x-ruststream-amqp extension lists each binding of a subscription: exchange, type, routing key and arguments, in declaration order. The specification's channel binding is a queue or a routing key, and it has no field for what joins the two. So a subscription reports its bindings in this crate's extension, beside the amqp binding of its channel. The extension holds a bindings list with one entry per bind and bind_with, in the order the descriptor declares them. An entry carries the exchange name and its type: direct, fanout, headers, topic, or the type a plugin exchange declares. The routingKey is written even when it is empty, because an empty key is the binding key of a fanout or a headers exchange. The arguments appear when the binding has any, each value in the JSON shape of its AMQP type. A subscription with no binding has no extension. An extension is not a binding, so it carries no bindingVersion.

The queue inventory.events is bound to a topic exchange by its key and to a headers exchange by its arguments. Macros Manual examples/lapin_asyncapi.rs /// What a headers exchange matches a binding on: every entry, or any one of them. fn gold_tier() -> FieldTable { let mut arguments = FieldTable::default(); arguments.insert("x-match".into(), AMQPValue::LongString("all".into())); arguments.insert("tier".into(), AMQPValue::LongString("gold".into())); arguments } #[subscriber( RabbitQueue::new("inventory.events") .bind(RabbitExchange::topic("events"), "inventory.*") .bind_with(RabbitExchange::headers("attributes"), "", gold_tier()) )] async fn on_event(event: &Event, Out(restocks): Out<impl Publisher, Restocks>) -> HandlerOutcome { if event.in_stock > 0 { return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } let restock = Restock { sku: event.sku.clone(), }; if restocks.message(&restock).publish().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/lapin_asyncapi.rs /// What a headers exchange matches a binding on: every entry, or any one of them. fn gold_tier() -> FieldTable { let mut arguments = FieldTable::default(); arguments.insert("x-match".into(), AMQPValue::LongString("all".into())); arguments.insert("tier".into(), AMQPValue::LongString("gold".into())); arguments } /// The events queue, fed by a topic exchange and by a headers exchange. fn events() -> RabbitQueue { RabbitQueue::new("inventory.events") .bind(RabbitExchange::topic("events"), "inventory.*") .bind_with(RabbitExchange::headers("attributes"), "", gold_tier()) } The service's document, in excerpt: the extension sits under the channel inventory.events. A test holds the service to every value of the excerpt. tests/snapshots/asyncapi-amqp.json { "servers": { "rabbit": { "host": "rabbit:5672", "protocol": "amqp", "protocolVersion": "0.9.1" } }, "channels": { "inventory.check": { "address": "inventory.check", "bindings": { "amqp": { "is": "queue", "queue": { "name": "inventory.check", "durable": false, "exclusive": true, "autoDelete": true }, "bindingVersion": "0.3.0" } } }, "inventory.events": { "address": "inventory.events", "bindings": { "amqp": { "is": "queue", "queue": { "name": "inventory.events" }, "bindingVersion": "0.3.0" }, "x-ruststream-amqp": { "bindings": [ { "exchange": "events", "type": "topic", "routingKey": "inventory.*" }, { "exchange": "attributes", "type": "headers", "routingKey": "", "arguments": { "x-match": "all", "tier": "gold" } } ] } } }, "inventory.unrouted": { "address": null, "bindings": { "amqp": { "is": "routingKey", "exchange": { "name": "answers" }, "bindingVersion": "0.3.0" } } }, "inventory.dead": { "address": "inventory.dead", "bindings": { "amqp": { "is": "queue", "queue": { "name": "inventory.dead" }, "bindingVersion": "0.3.0" } } } }, "operations": { "receive_inventory_check": { "action": "receive", "bindings": { "amqp": { "ack": true, "bindingVersion": "0.3.0" } }, "reply": { "address": { "location": "$message.header#/reply-to" } } }, "send_inventory_check_inventory_dead": { "action": "send", "bindings": { "amqp": { "deliveryMode": 2, "bindingVersion": "0.3.0" } } } } }

A receive operation reports manual acknowledgement; a send reports the delivery mode, priority and expiration its policy fixes. Every receive operation carries ack: true. This crate acknowledges each delivery by hand, so the handler's outcome settles it. A slot entry and a dead-letter destination each have a send operation. Its binding carries the properties every message through the policy takes. deliveryMode is 2, persistent, unless the policy sets persistent(false), which gives 1. priority and expiration, in milliseconds, appear when the policy fixes a priority or an expiration. The document describes the declaration, so a step that adjusts one message leaves it as it is. A reply is the reply of its receive operation. Under DirectReplyTo the reply's address has the location $message.header#/reply-to: a client reads the address from the request's reply-to header.

The operation receive_inventory_check reports ack: true and a reply addressed by reply-to. The operation send_inventory_events_inventory_restock reports delivery mode 2, priority 4 and an expiration of 30000. The server reports the host and the AMQP version; the credentials and the virtual host of the connection URI stay in the service. A broker registered with with_broker_labeled is a server of the document, under its label. Its host is the host and port of the connection URI. The user, the password, the virtual host and the query of the URI stay out of it. A URI with no port gives the host alone. The protocol is amqp, and protocolVersion is 0.9.1. AMQP 1.0 is a different protocol with a binding of its own, so the version tells a reader which one a client speaks here.

The broker connects as the user inventory to the virtual host prod. Its server in the document is rabbit:5672, protocol amqp, version 0.9.1. Macros Manual examples/lapin_asyncapi.rs /// The production server: the URI carries the service's credentials and its virtual host. fn broker(password: &str) -> LapinBroker { LapinBroker::new(format!("amqp://inventory:{password}@rabbit:5672/prod")) } examples/manual/lapin_asyncapi.rs /// The production server: the URI carries the service's credentials and its virtual host. fn broker(password: &str) -> LapinBroker { LapinBroker::new(format!("amqp://inventory:{password}@rabbit:5672/prod")) }

LapinBroker connects a service to RabbitMQ; new only records the URI, and the runtime connects it at startup and shuts it down at the end. LapinBroker::new takes the connection URI. It does no I/O, so the whole service fits the synchronous #[ruststream::app] builder. The settings that follow it are builder steps too: a connection name, a default prefetch window and declare_topology. At startup the runtime connects the broker and receives a ConnectedLapinBroker. The connect opens the AMQP connection and logs in, so an unreachable server or a refused login fails startup instead of the first delivery. Every subscription and every publisher of the service opens against that connected form. At shutdown the runtime closes the connection and receives a ClosedLapinBroker. #[subscriber("orders")] consumes the queue orders. The queue has to exist on the server, unless the broker declares the topology. The descriptors that bind a queue to an exchange or choose its type are on the Subscriptions pages.

The service consumes the queue orders on a server at localhost:5672. cargo run --example lapin_broker_service --features testing -- run starts it. Macros Manual examples/lapin_broker_service.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; #[subscriber("orders")] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(place); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_broker_service.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Place).build()); }, ) }

The URI carries the credentials, the virtual host and the scheme; connection_name labels the service in the management UI. The URI has the form amqp://user:password@host:port/vhost. A URI without credentials logs in as guest, and RabbitMQ admits guest only from localhost. A URI without a virtual host connects to the default one, /. The amqps scheme opens the connection over TLS. A URI that does not parse fails startup with AmqpError::Connect, in a test as on a server. connection_name is the name the management UI lists for the connection. A connection without one is listed by its client address and port. One connection carries the whole service. Each subscription opens a channel of its own on it. Fire-and-forget publishes share one channel. A confirms or server-transaction publisher opens its own channel on first use, because both modes are channel state.

Recovery is off by default. Enable it with auto_recover(true). Lapin restores the connection, channels, declared exchanges, queues, bindings, prefetch, publisher confirms and consumers. Existing handles stay usable; the application and its startup hooks do not restart. Retries use Lapin's exponential backoff. The default limit is 16 retries, configurable with recovery_retries(n). The limit applies to the initial connection and later reconnects. Zero allows an attempt without retrying; a successful connection resets the retry budget. With recovery off, the initial connection is attempted once. Exhausting startup retries returns AmqpError::Connect; exhausting recovery ends the affected consumer stream with AmqpError::Consume. Set a heartbeat in the URI, such as ?heartbeat=30, so RabbitMQ and Lapin can detect silent connection loss. ConnectedLapinBroker::is_connected() is a synchronous connection check for readiness: it is false while disconnected or after shutdown. A true result does not guarantee that channel and topology restoration has finished, or that workers are healthy. Lapin can restore a publisher channel before another channel has recreated an exclusive queue and its binding. A publish in that window can be confirmed but unroutable: RabbitMQ discards it, so it is neither queued nor redelivered. Publisher confirms alone do not prove that a route exists. Keep production topology provisioned independently of the reconnecting connection, or establish that the route is ready before sending application messages. This cross-channel recovery ordering is tracked in Lapin issue #481. A failed publish is not replayed, outstanding RPC deadlines keep running, and server transactions require recovery to remain disabled.

The service logs in as orders on the virtual host shop, enables recovery with 32 retries, and requests a 30-second heartbeat. Macros Manual examples/lapin_broker_connection.rs /// The user `orders` on the virtual host `shop`; the management UI lists the connection as /// `orders-svc`. fn broker() -> LapinBroker { LapinBroker::new("amqp://orders:secret@localhost:5672/shop?heartbeat=30") .connection_name("orders-svc") .auto_recover(true) .recovery_retries(32) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker(), |b| { b.include(place); }) } examples/manual/lapin_broker_connection.rs /// The user `orders` on the virtual host `shop`; the management UI lists the connection as /// `orders-svc`. fn broker() -> LapinBroker { LapinBroker::new("amqp://orders:secret@localhost:5672/shop?heartbeat=30") .connection_name("orders-svc") .auto_recover(true) .recovery_retries(32) } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Place).build()); }) }

declare_topology(true) declares the exchanges, the queue and the bindings a descriptor states; off, the topology is the operator's and must exist. The setting is off by default. A descriptor then states the topology the service expects, and the service creates nothing. A subscription to a queue the server does not have fails startup with AmqpError::Subscribe. With the setting on, each subscription declares its topology before it starts consuming. It declares the exchanges its bindings name, then the queue, then the bindings, in that order. The built-in amq.* exchanges and the default exchange are never declared: the server already has them. A declaration repeats safely while the descriptor matches what the server holds. A queue or an exchange declared again with other settings is refused by the server with PRECONDITION_FAILED, and startup fails with AmqpError::Declare. RabbitMQ 4 refuses a transient queue that is not exclusive, so a RabbitQueue declared durable(false) has to be exclusive(true) too. Some settings exist only as declaration arguments, so they reach the server only from a service that declares. A quorum queue's delivery limit and the waiting queue of a delayed redelivery are two of them. The in-process transport finds every queue a subscription names, so a test shows no missing queue. A declaration the server refuses is refused in process too.

The service declares the topic exchange events, the queue orders and the binding order.* between them. Macros Manual examples/lapin_broker_declare_topology.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders").bind(RabbitExchange::topic("events"), "order.*"))] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { // The service owns `events`, `orders` and the binding between them. let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(place); }) } examples/manual/lapin_broker_declare_topology.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { // The service owns `events`, `orders` and the binding between them. let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let orders = RabbitQueue::new("orders").bind(RabbitExchange::topic("events"), "order.*"); b.include(subscriber(orders, Place).build()); }) }

AmqpError is the crate's one error: connect, publish, subscribe, consume, declare, request, timeout, closed, transaction and options. Each variant names the step that failed. The lapin error behind it is its source, so the client library's types stay out of the crate's API. Variant When Connect the URI did not parse, the server was unreachable or refused the login, or the close failed Publish the server refused a message, such as a body over its 16 MiB max_message_size, or did not confirm it Subscribe a channel, its prefetch or its consumer could not be opened, such as on a queue the server does not have Consume an open consumer failed to receive Declare the server refused an exchange, a queue or a binding the service declares Request a request could not be sent, or its reply could not be received RequestTimeout no reply arrived within the requester's deadline Closed a publisher or a requester was used after the shutdown; it names the target Transaction a transaction call came out of order: a commit with none open, or a second begin InvalidOptions the settings cannot work together, such as half of a quorum queue's retry declaration A service meets the error in two places. A failed startup carries it as the source of the runtime's error, and the service exits before it consumes anything. A publish from a handler returns it inside the core's PublishError, and the handler decides how the delivery settles. The enum is #[non_exhaustive], so a match on it ends with a wildcard arm. With automatic recovery enabled, transient disconnects pause consumers. When retries run out, a consumer stream yields a terminal AmqpError::Consume and ends. Pairing ServerTxPublish with auto_recover(true) fails with AmqpError::InvalidOptions; direct server-transaction operations reject that combination too.

A shipment the server refuses is logged with its cause, and the order is dropped to the queue's dead-letter exchange. Macros Manual examples/lapin_broker_errors.rs #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders").dead_letter_exchange("orders.failed"))] async fn ship(order: &Order, Out(shipments): Out<impl Publisher, Shipments>) -> HandlerOutcome { let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id, labels: (1..=order.parcels) .map(|parcel| format!("{}-{parcel:07}", order.id)) .collect(), }; if let Err(err) = shipments.message(&shipment).publish().await { // The error names the step that failed and the server's reason. tracing::warn!(subscription = "orders", order.id, error = %err, "shipment not published"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/lapin_broker_errors.rs struct Ship; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Ship where Entry: OutEntry<Shipments, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id, labels: (1..=order.parcels) .map(|parcel| format!("{}-{parcel:07}", order.id)) .collect(), }; if let Err(err) = outs.get(Shipments).message(&shipment).publish().await { // The error names the step that failed and the server's reason. tracing::warn!(subscription = "orders", order.id, error = %err, "shipment not published"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } Ok(()) } } fn orders() -> RabbitQueue { RabbitQueue::new("orders").dead_letter_exchange("orders.failed") }

One glob, ruststream_lapin::prelude, brings the core prelude, the descriptors, the policies under the family's names and the context keys. use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; is the one import a RabbitMQ routes file writes. It carries the core's own prelude, so #[subscriber], RustStream, HandlerOutcome and Out come with it. It adds LapinBroker, the descriptors RabbitQueue and RabbitQuorumQueue, RabbitExchange, Delay and DirectReplyTo. It adds the context keys Exchange, RoutingKey, Redelivered and DeliveryTag, and the argument types AMQPValue and FieldTable. It also carries the transaction traits a handler settles a transaction with. The publish policies come under the names every broker crate uses: Publish is LapinPublish, TransactionalPublish is ConfirmsPublish, and Request is LapinRequest. So a mount site reads the same on every broker. ServerTxPublish keeps its own name: an AMQP server transaction is a guarantee of its own, not a second spelling of TransactionalPublish. Two broker preludes in one file collide on the uniform names; the prefixed types at the crate root tell them apart. A handler body bounds its slots with capability traits, such as Out<impl TransactionalPublisher>, and names no broker type. The one exception is a body that sets an AMQP property for a single message: it bounds its slot Out<impl Publisher<Options = LapinPublishOptions>, Marker> and calls the steps of LapinPublishSteps, both from this prelude.

The routes file reads the routing key through a context key and replies through TransactionalPublish, all from the one glob. Macros Manual examples/lapin_broker_prelude.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; #[subscriber( RabbitQueue::new("orders").bind(RabbitExchange::topic("events"), "order.*"), reply )] async fn confirm(order: &Order, Ctx(routing_key): Ctx<RoutingKey>) -> Confirmation { tracing::info!(order.id, %routing_key, "order confirmed"); Confirmation { id: order.id } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(confirm) .out_reply(TransactionalPublish::default()); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_broker_prelude.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmation, (), AmqpContext> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, AmqpContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { let routing_key = ctx.context(RoutingKey); tracing::info!(order.id, %routing_key, "order confirmed"); ready(Ok(Confirmation { id: order.id })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { let orders = RabbitQueue::new("orders").bind(RabbitExchange::topic("events"), "order.*"); b.include(subscriber(orders, Confirm).reply().build()) .out_reply(TransactionalPublish::default()); }, ) }

A publisher or requester that outlives the connection reports AmqpError::Closed instead of succeeding against a closed connection. At shutdown the runtime stops the subscriptions and lets the handlers in flight finish. Then it closes the connection with the AMQP close handshake. A delivery the service received and never settled goes back to its queue when its channel closes, so another consumer gets it. A publisher handed out before the shutdown can outlive it: a task the service spawned keeps it, or a clone of a requester does. Every use of such a handle after the shutdown returns AmqpError::Closed, which names the routing key, the queue or the exchange the call targeted. The connection is marked closed before the handshake starts, so no message slips into a connection that is going away. A tool that drives the broker by hand receives a ClosedLapinBroker from the shutdown; its handshake tells an orderly close from a connection the server had already dropped. If shutdown starts during a reconnect, it marks the broker closed and wakes waiting consumers without waiting for RabbitMQ to return. Existing publishers and requesters then return AmqpError::Closed. If Lapin reconnects afterward, the connection is closed in the background; if retries run out, cleanup ends. No AMQP close handshake is reported for a connection that was unavailable at shutdown.

A heartbeat task takes its publisher at startup and runs past the service's shutdown; its first publish after the shutdown fails with AmqpError::Closed, and the task ends. Macros Manual examples/lapin_broker_shutdown.rs /// Announces the service every 30 seconds until a publish fails; after shutdown that failure is /// `AmqpError::Closed`. async fn heartbeat(publisher: LapinPublisher) { let mut ticks = interval(Duration::from_secs(30)); loop { ticks.tick().await; let beat = Heartbeat { service: "orders".to_owned(), }; if let Err(err) = publisher.message(&beat).publish().await { tracing::info!(error = %err, "heartbeat stopped"); return; } } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(place); // The task keeps its publisher past the service's shutdown. b.after_startup(Publish::default(), async move |publisher| { tokio::spawn(heartbeat(publisher)); Ok::<_, Infallible>(()) }); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_broker_shutdown.rs /// Announces the service every 30 seconds until a publish fails; after shutdown that failure is /// `AmqpError::Closed`. async fn heartbeat(publisher: LapinPublisher) { let mut ticks = interval(Duration::from_secs(30)); loop { ticks.tick().await; let beat = Heartbeat { service: "orders".to_owned(), }; if let Err(err) = publisher.message(&beat).publish().await { tracing::info!(error = %err, "heartbeat stopped"); return; } } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Place).build()); // The task keeps its publisher past the service's shutdown. b.after_startup(Publish::default(), async move |publisher| { tokio::spawn(heartbeat(publisher)); Ok::<_, Infallible>(()) }); }, ) }

An amqps URI with one of the tls-native-tls, tls-rustls or tls-rustls-ring features connects over TLS, through lapin's own backends. Each feature turns on one TLS backend of the lapin client: Feature Backend tls-native-tls the platform's TLS library: OpenSSL on Linux, Secure Transport on macOS, SChannel on Windows tls-rustls rustls with the aws-lc-rs crypto provider, checking the server against the platform's trusted roots tls-rustls-ring rustls with the ring crypto provider A service enables one of them on its ruststream-lapin dependency, for example features = ["tls-rustls"]. RabbitMQ listens for TLS on port 5671 by default, so an amqps URI usually names that port. The URI keeps the form of a plain connection: credentials, host, port and virtual host. The handshake happens when the runtime connects the broker at startup. A certificate the client does not trust fails startup with AmqpError::Connect. The in-process transport opens no socket: it parses the amqps URI as the real connect does and runs the service's handlers without a handshake.

The service connects to rabbit.example.com over TLS, as the user orders on the virtual host shop. Ctx keys give a handler the exchange, routing key, redelivered flag and delivery tag; Context<'_, AmqpContext> reads them all. AmqpContext carries what a delivery has beside its payload and its headers. The subscription builds it once per delivery. A handler binds one field with Ctx<K>, where K is a key of context::keys: Key Value What it is Exchange String the exchange the message was published to, empty for the default exchange RoutingKey String the routing key the message was published with Redelivered bool whether the server handed the message out before DeliveryTag u64 the delivery's number on its channel The four keys are in the prelude. A body that reads several fields takes ctx: &mut Context<'_, AmqpContext> instead and calls ctx.context(key) per field, as the manual form does; there the exchange and the routing key are borrowed &str. AmqpContext itself comes from ruststream_lapin::context. The routing key tells apart the messages a topic binding takes. Redelivered is set on a delivery a classic queue hands out again after a retry; a quorum queue counts deliveries instead. The delivery tag numbers the deliveries of one channel, so it identifies a delivery only within its subscription.

The handler replies with where each order came from. Macros Manual examples/lapin_context.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; /// Records where each order came from: its exchange and routing key, and whether the server had /// handed it out before. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"), reply)] async fn audit( order: &Order, Ctx(exchange): Ctx<Exchange>, Ctx(routing_key): Ctx<RoutingKey>, Ctx(redelivered): Ctx<Redelivered>, Ctx(delivery_tag): Ctx<DeliveryTag>, ) -> AuditRecord { tracing::info!(order.id, %exchange, %routing_key, redelivered, delivery_tag, "order audited"); AuditRecord { order_id: order.id, exchange, routing_key, redelivered, } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(audit).out_reply(Publish::default()); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_context.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; /// Records where each order came from: its exchange and routing key, and whether the server had /// handed it out before. struct Audit; impl Handle<Order, AuditRecord, (), AmqpContext> for Audit { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, AmqpContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<AuditRecord, HandlerOutcome>> { let exchange = ctx.context(Exchange); let routing_key = ctx.context(RoutingKey); let redelivered = ctx.context(Redelivered); let delivery_tag = ctx.context(DeliveryTag); tracing::info!(order.id, %exchange, %routing_key, redelivered, delivery_tag, "order audited"); ready(Ok(AuditRecord { order_id: order.id, exchange: exchange.to_owned(), routing_key: routing_key.to_owned(), redelivered, })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { let orders = RabbitQueue::new("orders"); b.include(subscriber(orders, Audit).reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish::default()); }, ) }

bind joins a queue to a RabbitExchange under a routing key; a direct exchange routes on the exact key, and the default exchange on queue names. A publisher sends a message to an exchange, never to a queue. The exchange copies the message into the queues bound to it whose bindings match. RabbitExchange names the exchange of a binding, and its constructor names its type: Constructor Routes on direct the exact routing key topic a dotted pattern of the routing key fanout nothing: every bound queue gets every message headers the message's headers, against the binding's arguments consistent_hash a hash of the routing key, through a plugin bind(exchange, routing_key) adds a binding to a queue descriptor, and a queue may carry several. A direct exchange delivers a message to every queue bound under its routing key exactly; a message under a key no queue is bound under goes nowhere. The default exchange, with the empty name, is a direct exchange every queue is bound to under its own name. So a message published with no exchange reaches the queue its routing key names, and a binding to the default exchange is refused. An exchange is durable by default and survives a broker restart, and auto_delete is off. The exchange and its bindings reach the server when the broker declares the topology; the built-in amq.* exchanges are bound to and never declared. The publishing side names its exchange on the publish policy with exchange, and the message's name is its routing key. RabbitExchange::custom(name, kind) names an exchange of a type a server plugin provides, such as x-random or x-modulus-hash. A queue binds to it with bind, or with bind_with for a plugin that routes on binding arguments. The plugin does the routing, so the server needs the plugin enabled, and the in-process transport routes nothing through such an exchange.

Checkout publishes each payment to the direct exchange payments under its method; the card queue is bound under card, the invoice queue under invoice. bind_with binds a queue to a headers exchange by x-match and the headers to match, all of them or any one. A headers exchange ignores the routing key and routes on the message's headers. bind_with(exchange, routing_key, arguments) gives the binding an argument table, a FieldTable of AMQPValue entries. The entry x-match decides the rule: all takes a message that carries every other entry of the table with the same value, and any takes a message that carries at least one. The other entries are the headers to match, and the routing key of the binding is usually empty. A plain bind to a headers exchange sends an empty table, and all of no headers is true of every message, so such a queue gets everything the exchange gets. The publishing side sets the headers on the message, and they ride the AMQP header table the exchange reads. bind_with also serves a plugin exchange that routes on binding arguments.

The EU gold queue matches both headers, and the EU-or-gold queue matches either one. arguments.insert("x-match".into(), AMQPValue::LongString(x_match.into())); arguments.insert("region".into(), AMQPValue::LongString("eu".into())); arguments.insert("tier".into(), AMQPValue::LongString("gold".into())); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Orders from the EU or of the gold tier: one header is enough. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders.eu-or-gold") .bind_with(RabbitExchange::headers("orders"), "", gold_in_eu("any")))] async fn review(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "reviewed"); consistent_hash spreads a stream over queues bound with integer weights, by a hash of the routing key, through the RabbitMQ plugin. The constructor exists with the crate's plugin-consistent-hash feature and names the x-consistent-hash type of the rabbitmq_consistent_hash_exchange plugin. The server needs the plugin enabled: rabbitmq-plugins enable rabbitmq_consistent_hash_exchange. Each queue binds with its weight as the routing key, such as "1" or "2", and takes that share of the hash space. The exchange hashes the routing key of each message, so messages with one key always reach the same queue. So a key such as a customer or an account keeps its messages in one queue, in order, while the stream spreads over all of them. Within one service instance, lanes give the same per-key order without the plugin. The plugin does the routing on the server. The in-process transport declares the exchange and its bindings and routes nothing through it, so a test of the spread runs against a plugin-enabled server with TestApp::start_live.

Orders are hashed by customer over two shards of equal weight. Macros Manual examples/lapin_exchanges_consistent_hash.rs /// Two shards of equal weight: the binding key is the weight, and one customer's orders always /// land on the same shard. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders.shard-a") .bind(RabbitExchange::consistent_hash("orders-by-customer"), "1"))] async fn shard_a(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, order.customer, "shard a"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders.shard-b") .bind(RabbitExchange::consistent_hash("orders-by-customer"), "1"))] async fn shard_b(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, order.customer, "shard b"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/lapin_exchanges_consistent_hash.rs struct ShardA; impl Handle<Order> for ShardA { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, order.customer, "shard a"); ready(Ok(())) } } struct ShardB; impl Handle<Order> for ShardB { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, order.customer, "shard b"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// Two shards of equal weight: the binding key is the weight, and one customer's orders always /// land on the same shard. fn shards() -> (RabbitQueue, RabbitQueue) { let by_customer = RabbitExchange::consistent_hash("orders-by-customer"); let a = RabbitQueue::new("orders.shard-a").bind(by_customer.clone(), "1"); let b = RabbitQueue::new("orders.shard-b").bind(by_customer, "1"); (a, b) }

A fanout exchange copies every message to every bound queue and ignores the routing key. A queue binds to a fanout exchange with any routing key, usually the empty one. Each bound queue gets its own copy, and each copy is consumed and settled on its own. So a fanout exchange is the broadcast of RabbitMQ: one event, many independent consumers. A service that needs a copy in every instance binds an exclusive queue per instance.

A price change reaches both the search index and the cache, each through a queue of its own. A topic exchange routes on dotted routing-key patterns, where * matches one word and # any number of words. A routing key of a topic exchange is a list of words separated by dots, such as order.created or order.shipped.late. A queue binds with a pattern of the same shape. * stands for exactly one word, and # for zero or more words. So order.* takes order.created and passes order.shipped.late by, and order.# takes both. A pattern without wildcards matches its key exactly, as on a direct exchange. A message that matches several bindings of one queue reaches that queue once. A handler that serves several keys reads the key of each delivery through the RoutingKey context key.

tracing::info!(event.id, %key, "order event audited"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// Only the shipments. struct NotifyShipping; impl Handle<OrderEvent> for NotifyShipping { fn handle( &self, event: &OrderEvent, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(event.id, "shipping notified"); LapinPublish, Publish in the prelude, is the fire-and-forget publish policy: a publish resolves once the frame is written, with no broker confirm. The message name is the routing key, and the exchange belongs to the policy. By default that is the default exchange, where a routing key addresses the queue of the same name; exchange names another. The policy holds no connection. At startup the runtime pairs it with the connected broker into a LapinPublisher, which publishes on the connection's shared publish channel. A publisher kept past shutdown answers every publish with AmqpError::Closed. A mount site names the policy wherever a registration publishes: .out_reply(Publish::default()) for a reply, .out(Slot, Publish::default()) for a slot, .out_retry(Publish::default()) for retry copies. It is also the broker's default policy, so a registration that names none replies and retries through it. Where a reply goes is a property of the reply type, as the core's replies page describes. A publish outside a handler goes through after_startup on the broker scope: once the subscriptions are open, the runtime pairs the policy and hands the hook the live publisher. The policy holds the defaults of the per-message properties. confirms and server_tx move to the transactional policies and keep these settings. Automatic recovery restores publisher channels and confirms, but does not replay failed publishes. A publish during an outage can return an error, and the outcome of an in-flight publish can be uncertain. An application that retries must account for possible duplicates. Connection readiness alone does not mean every publisher channel has finished recovering. A recovered publisher channel can also precede binding restoration on another channel; a confirmed publish can then be unroutable and discarded, as described under connection recovery.

Every order is answered with a confirmation, routed under the name the reply type declares. Once its subscriptions are open, the service announces itself. Macros Manual examples/lapin_publishing_publish.rs /// Every order is answered with a confirmation, routed under the name its type declares. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"), reply)] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); Confirmation { order_id: order.id } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(confirm).out_reply(Publish::default()); // Once the subscriptions are open, the service announces itself. b.after_startup(Publish::default(), async move |publisher| { let started = Started { service: "orders".into(), }; publisher.message(&started).publish().await }); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_publishing_publish.rs /// Every order is answered with a confirmation, routed under the name its type declares. struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmation> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); ready(Ok(Confirmation { order_id: order.id })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { let confirm = subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"), Confirm); b.include(confirm.reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish::default()); // Once the subscriptions are open, the service announces itself. b.after_startup(Publish::default(), async move |publisher| { let started = Started { service: "orders".into(), }; publisher.message(&started).publish().await }); }, ) }

exchange sends a policy's publishes to a named exchange instead of the default exchange. The message name stays the routing key, and the exchange routes by it. A topic exchange matches it against binding patterns, a direct exchange matches it exactly, and a fanout exchange ignores it. Without exchange, the default exchange delivers to the queue whose name equals the routing key. RabbitMQ accepts a publish that matches no binding and drops it. Every publish policy of the crate takes the setting: ConfirmsPublish, ServerTxPublish and LapinRequest too. With declare_topology(true), the subscription that binds a queue to the exchange declares the exchange.

Every accepted order is announced on the events topic exchange under order.placed. An audit queue bound under order.* receives it.
