let events = outs.get(DefaultSlot); if events.message(&placed).publish().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } /// The audit service's queue takes every `order.*` event from that exchange. struct Audit; impl Handle<OrderPlaced> for Audit { fn handle( &self, placed: &OrderPlaced, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(placed.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let audit = RabbitQueue::new("orders.audit").bind(RabbitExchange::topic("events"), "order.*"); b.include(subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"), Accept).build()) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish::default().exchange("events")) .build(); b.include(subscriber(audit, Audit).build()); }) }

A publish's headers travel in the AMQP frame: content-type, correlation-id, reply-to and message-id ride the native properties of those names, and every other header lands in the header table. A handler hands the headers to the publish builder with .with_headers(..), as a HeaderMap or as the typed contract its message declares. The four identity headers become properties, so a consumer written against another client finds them where the protocol puts them. Every other header is a byte string in the header table, so a binary value survives the round trip. A delivery reports both kinds back as headers, and the handler reads them from its context. A delivery also reports two properties under headers of their own: the priority under PRIORITY_HEADER (amqp-priority) and the TTL under EXPIRATION_HEADER (amqp-expiration). A header never sets a delivery property: priority, expiration and delivery mode are properties of the policy and the publish builder. An AMQP property is a short string of at most 255 bytes, and a longer identity header fails the publish with AmqpError::InvalidOptions before anything is routed.

The invoice carries the order's reference as its message-id property and the tenant in the header table. The billing side reads both from its context. Macros Manual examples/lapin_publishing_headers.rs /// The invoice carries the order's reference as its `message-id` property and the tenant in the /// header table. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"))] async fn issue_invoice(order: &Order, Out(invoices): Out<impl Publisher>) -> HandlerOutcome { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); headers.insert("message-id", order.reference.clone()); headers.insert("tenant", "acme"); let invoice = Invoice { order_id: order.id }; if let Err(err) = invoices .message(&invoice) .with_headers(headers) .publish() .await { // A reference longer than a short string is refused, and a retry will not shorten it. tracing::error!(order.id, %err, "invoice refused"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The billing side reads both where it reads every header. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("invoices"))] async fn bill(invoice: &Invoice, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { let reference = ctx.headers().get_str("message-id").unwrap_or_default(); let tenant = ctx.headers().get_str("tenant").unwrap_or_default(); tracing::info!(invoice.order_id, reference, tenant, "invoice billed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(issue_invoice) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish::default()) .build(); b.include(bill); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_publishing_headers.rs /// The invoice carries the order's reference as its `message-id` property and the tenant in the /// header table. struct IssueInvoice; LapinPublishSteps adds priority, expiration and persistent to the publish builder, so a handler sets an AMQP property of one message. A publish policy holds the defaults for every message it sends, and a step adjusts one message over them. LapinPublishOptions holds the three settings, each optional: what a call leaves alone keeps the policy's value. The steps exist on a publisher whose options type is LapinPublishOptions. So the handler bounds its slot Out<impl Publisher<Options = LapinPublishOptions>, Slot> and still names no publisher type. The steps come from this crate's prelude, the one prelude a handler body imports besides the framework's. The values reach the frame as protocol fields, never as headers. The publish still leaves through the slot's own entry, with its codec and transforms. A test reads the options back with with_options on tb.out::<Slot>().

expiration gives one message a time to live; LapinPublish::expiration gives one to every message of a policy. A message nobody consumed within its TTL leaves the queue. The broker drops it, or dead-letters it where the queue has a dead-letter exchange. RabbitMQ expires a message when it reaches the head of its queue. A policy that sets no TTL sends messages that do not expire. AMQP counts the TTL in whole milliseconds, and a shorter non-zero TTL becomes one millisecond. A delivery reports it under EXPIRATION_HEADER in milliseconds.

persistent sets the delivery mode of one message; LapinPublish::persistent sets it for every message of a policy. A persistent message (delivery mode 2) on a durable queue survives a broker restart. A transient message (delivery mode 1) does not. The publish policies default to persistent. LapinRequest defaults to transient: a request nobody waits for after its timeout gains nothing from a restart.

priority sets the AMQP priority of one message; LapinPublish::priority sets it for every message of a policy. A policy that sets no priority sends none. RabbitMQ orders deliveries by priority only on a queue declared with x-max-priority, and a higher priority counts as that maximum. On any other queue the priority travels to the consumer and orders nothing. A delivery reports it under PRIORITY_HEADER as decimal digits, and the handler reads it like any other header. A delayed redelivery keeps the priority its original delivery reported.

LapinRequest, Request in the prelude, gives a handler a requester: it publishes a request over RabbitMQ direct reply-to and awaits the correlated reply. The handler bounds its slot Out<impl RequestReply> and calls request with a message and a timeout. At startup the runtime pairs the policy into a LapinRequester. Each request goes out with reply-to set to the amq.rabbitmq.reply-to pseudo-queue and a generated correlation-id. The reply that carries that id resolves the call, and a reply with an id nobody waits for is dropped. No reply within the timeout fails the call with AmqpError::RequestTimeout. One task per requester reads the replies, started by its first request on the runtime the broker connected on. The request carries bytes, so the example encodes the question and decodes the answer with the core's JSON codec. The policy takes exchange, priority and expiration like a publish policy. Requests are transient by default, and persistent(true) makes them persistent. Direct reply-to is at-most-once: the reply state lives on the requester's channel on one node, and nothing is queued durably. A channel that drops loses the replies in flight, and the caller sees a timeout. The responder is any service that answers at the received reply-to with the same correlation-id, as DirectReplyTo does.

An order asks the inventory service whether its item is in stock. An order in stock is accepted, one out of stock is dropped, and no answer brings the order back. Macros Manual examples/lapin_request_request.rs /// Asks the inventory service whether `sku` is in stock, and waits two seconds at most. async fn in_stock( inventory: &impl RequestReply, sku: &str, ) -> Result<bool, Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> { let request = JsonCodec.encode(&CheckStock { sku: sku.to_owned(), })?; let ask = OutgoingMessage::new("inventory.check", request.as_ref()); let reply = inventory.request(ask, Duration::from_secs(2)).await?; let stock: Stock = JsonCodec.decode(reply.payload())?; Ok(stock.available) } /// An order in stock is accepted and one out of stock is dropped. An inventory service that does /// not answer brings the order back. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"))] async fn place_order(order: &Order, Out(inventory): Out<impl RequestReply>) -> HandlerOutcome { match in_stock(inventory, &order.sku).await { Ok(true) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Ok(false) => HandlerOutcome::drop(), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(order.id, %err, "inventory unavailable"); HandlerOutcome::retry() } } } examples/manual/lapin_request_request.rs /// Asks the inventory service whether `sku` is in stock, and waits two seconds at most. async fn in_stock( inventory: &impl RequestReply, sku: &str, ) -> Result<bool, Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> { let request = JsonCodec.encode(&CheckStock { sku: sku.to_owned(), })?; let ask = OutgoingMessage::new("inventory.check", request.as_ref()); let reply = inventory.request(ask, Duration::from_secs(2)).await?; let stock: Stock = JsonCodec.decode(reply.payload())?; Ok(stock.available) } /// An order in stock is accepted and one out of stock is dropped. DirectReplyTo is a reply transform: it sends each reply to the address the request named in reply-to and echoes the request's correlation-id. It mounts on the reply position: .out_reply(policy).transform(DirectReplyTo). The handler is an ordinary reply handler and knows nothing about the requester. The transform names the destination of every reply, so it mounts only over a reply type that declares none. Over a type with its own #[outgoing(name = "..")] the mount does not compile. The name in the mount site's reply("..") is the fallback: a request without reply-to is answered there, and the generated AsyncAPI document reports it. A LapinRequest requester and a requester on another stack both name the reply address this way. With automatic recovery, the reply dispatcher resumes after Lapin restores its channel and direct reply-to consumer. Deadlines of requests already waiting for replies keep running during the outage; recovery does not restart them or replay their requests. A reply lost during a disconnect may therefore end in AmqpError::RequestTimeout.

The inventory service answers every stock check at the address the request named. A request without one is answered at inventory.check.unrouted. A handler's answer settles its AMQP delivery with a protocol frame: ack sends basic.ack, retry sends basic.reject with requeue, and drop sends basic.reject without it. The frame goes out on the channel the delivery arrived on, and the service publishes nothing. A requeued message goes back to its queue, which hands it out again with the redelivered flag set. The next delivery may reach this consumer or another consumer of the same queue. A handler reads the flag through the Redelivered key of the delivery context. A dropped message leaves the queue: RabbitMQ discards it, or routes it to the queue's dead-letter exchange. The crate settles with basic.reject and never with basic.nack. On one delivery the two frames do the same thing, but RabbitMQ counts a rejected delivery as spent and does not count a nacked one. So a handler that keeps asking for its message back runs down a quorum queue's delivery limit. A quorum queue stamps a returned message with the x-delivery-count header; a classic queue keeps no count, only the flag. A retry under a cap and a delayed retry travel as copies instead of a requeue. After a connection loss, a delivery's old acknowledgement belongs to the old channel and can fail even if the connection has recovered. RabbitMQ requeues unsettled messages from queues that survive the disconnect and may deliver them again. Do not treat reconnection as proof that the old delivery was settled; handlers must tolerate redelivery when recovery is enabled.

An order is requeued the first time it arrives and acknowledged when it comes back redelivered. An order without a SKU is dropped. Macros Manual examples/lapin_settlement_outcomes.rs /// An order without a SKU is rejected for good. Any other order is requeued once, the first time /// it arrives, and acknowledged when the queue hands it out again marked redelivered. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"))] async fn reserve(order: &Order, Ctx(redelivered): Ctx<Redelivered>) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.sku.is_empty() { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without a SKU, rejected"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } if !redelivered { tracing::info!(order.id, "stock not counted yet, back to the queue"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(order.id, "reserved"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("stock", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(reserve); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_settlement_outcomes.rs /// An order without a SKU is rejected for good. Any other order is requeued once, the first time /// it arrives, and acknowledged when the queue hands it out again marked redelivered. struct Reserve; impl Handle<Order, (), (), AmqpContext> for Reserve { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, AmqpContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let outcome = if order.sku.is_empty() { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without a SKU, rejected"); Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()) } else if !ctx.context(Redelivered) { tracing::info!(order.id, "stock not counted yet, back to the queue"); Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()) } else { tracing::info!(order.id, "reserved"); Ok(()) }; ready(outcome) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("stock", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"), Reserve).build()); }, ) }

dead_letter_exchange gives a queue its own route for the messages it rejects: the x-dead-letter-exchange argument. A drop settles with basic.reject without requeue, and the queue publishes the message to that exchange. The route belongs to the queue, so it takes every message the queue dead-letters, whatever the cause. Besides a rejection, RabbitMQ dead-letters a message whose TTL expired, one pushed out by a length limit, and one that spent a quorum queue's delivery limit. The message keeps its routing key, unless dead_letter_routing_key names another (x-dead-letter-routing-key). The dead-letter exchange routes like any other exchange: a queue bound to it under that key collects the messages. RabbitQuorumQueue takes the same two settings. Both settings are queue arguments. The queue gets them when the service declares it, with declare_topology(true) on the broker. A queue the operator provisions carries the arguments it was declared with. The dead_letter(name) step of the mount chain is a different thing: the destination of a registration's retry cap.

An invoice with a negative amount is dropped. The queue dead-letters it to invoices.dlx, where a second subscription reads it from the bound queue. delay(Delay::dlx_ttl()) makes retry_after wait on the broker: the copy parks in a waiting queue under a per-message TTL. On a retry_after, the crate publishes the copy to the waiting queue with the delay as its expiration, then acknowledges the original. Both frames go out on one channel in that order, so a connection lost between them brings the original back rather than losing it. The waiting queue has no consumers. When the TTL fires, it dead-letters the copy back to the origin queue on the default exchange. The copy lives on the broker, so it survives a restart of the service. The waiting queue is <queue>.retry; Delay::dlx_ttl_named names another. The released copy is a new message to the server, and it carries x-ruststream-retry-count raised by one. So a retry cap ends a delayed loop the way it ends an immediate one. A waiting queue releases expired messages only from its head, so a short delay waits behind a long one. Mixed delays take one waiting queue per delay class, or the delayed-message plugin. The waiting queue is infrastructure. With declare_topology(true) the service declares it: durable, dead-lettering to the origin queue. On a broker that declares nothing, the operator provisions it with those arguments. The subscription checks at startup that the waiting queue exists, and the service fails to start without it.

A shipment that arrives while the warehouse is closed waits a minute in shipments.retry. The released copy carries the retry count, and the shipment goes out. Macros Manual examples/lapin_settlement_delay.rs /// A shipment that arrives while the warehouse is closed waits a minute in `shipments.retry`, on /// the broker. The copy it releases carries the retry count, and the shipment goes out. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("shipments").delay(Delay::dlx_ttl()))] async fn dispatch(shipment: &Shipment, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { if ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).is_none() { tracing::info!(shipment.id, "warehouse closed, waiting"); return HandlerOutcome::retry_after(WAIT); } tracing::info!(shipment.id, "dispatched"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { // The service declares its queues, `shipments.retry` included. let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(dispatch); }) } examples/manual/lapin_settlement_delay.rs /// A shipment that arrives while the warehouse is closed waits a minute in `shipments.retry`, on /// the broker. The copy it releases carries the retry count, and the shipment goes out. struct Dispatch; impl Handle<Shipment> for Dispatch { fn handle( &self, shipment: &Shipment, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).is_none() { tracing::info!(shipment.id, "warehouse closed, waiting"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(WAIT))); } tracing::info!(shipment.id, "dispatched"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { // The service declares its queues, `shipments.retry` included. let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let shipments = RabbitQueue::new("shipments").delay(Delay::dlx_ttl()); b.include(subscriber(shipments, Dispatch).build()); }) }

delivery_limit(n) sets a quorum queue's x-delivery-limit: how many times the queue returns a message before it carries it away. The argument counts returns, so the queue delivers a message n + 1 times: delivery_limit(4) delivers it five times. A quorum queue counts a delivery the handler rejected and a delivery whose consumer went away without settling it. Once the count passes the limit, the queue sends the message to its dead-letter exchange, or drops it when it has none. The server applies the limit itself: it holds while no service is running, and the service publishes nothing. A quorum queue without a limit of its own takes RabbitMQ's default of 20 returns. A returned message carries the queue's count in the x-delivery-count header. A registration states the same through the mount chain: max_attempts(n) and dead_letter(name). On a quorum queue the pair becomes an x-delivery-limit of n - 1 and a dead-letter route to the queue name, written over the descriptor's limit. The pair reaches the queue only when the service declares it, so the broker sets declare_topology(true). On a broker that declares nothing the subscription refuses to start, and so does half of the pair. out_retry(policy) does not compile on a quorum queue, because no copy leaves this process.

The provider refuses a charge every time. The queue delivers it five times and then moves it to charges.dlx, where a classic queue keeps it. Macros Manual examples/lapin_settlement_delivery_limit.rs /// The provider refuses this charge every time. Delay::plugin_dme hands a delayed copy to RabbitMQ's delayed-message-exchange plugin instead of a waiting queue. The crate publishes the copy to an x-delayed-message exchange with the delay in its x-delay header, then acknowledges the original. The plugin holds each message for its own delay and then routes it to the origin queue. So a short delay never waits behind a long one, and one exchange serves every delay. The exchange is <queue>.delay; Delay::plugin_dme_named names another, which several queues may share. The released copy carries x-ruststream-retry-count raised by one, as with a waiting queue. The backend sits behind the crate's plugin-dme feature, and the plugin has to be enabled on the server. With declare_topology(true) the service declares the exchange and binds the origin queue to it. On a broker that declares nothing, the operator provisions both, and the subscription checks at startup that the exchange exists.

Each reminder waits as long as it asks for. The in-process transport releases the copy like a waiting queue; the plugin's own release order shows only against a server with the plugin. Macros Manual examples/lapin_settlement_plugin_dme.rs /// Each reminder waits as long as it asks, in the plugin's exchange `reminders.delay`. A short /// wait is released on time even while a long one is still held. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("reminders").delay(Delay::plugin_dme()))] async fn remind(reminder: &Reminder, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { if ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).is_none() { return HandlerOutcome::retry_after(Duration::from_secs(reminder.after_secs)); } tracing::info!(reminder.id, "reminder sent"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { // The service declares the delayed exchange; the plugin has to be enabled on the server. let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("reminders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(remind); }) } examples/manual/lapin_settlement_plugin_dme.rs /// Each reminder waits as long as it asks, in the plugin's exchange `reminders.delay`. A short /// wait is released on time even while a long one is still held. struct Remind; impl Handle<Reminder> for Remind { fn handle( &self, reminder: &Reminder, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).is_none() { let wait = Duration::from_secs(reminder.after_secs); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(wait))); } tracing::info!(reminder.id, "reminder sent"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { // The service declares the delayed exchange; the plugin has to be enabled on the server. let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("reminders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let reminders = RabbitQueue::new("reminders").delay(Delay::plugin_dme()); b.include(subscriber(reminders, Remind).build()); }) }

max_attempts(n) and dead_letter(name) cap the deliveries of one message; on a classic queue the runtime keeps the count. max_attempts(n) is how many deliveries one message gets, the first included. dead_letter(name) is where it goes once they run out. A classic queue counts nothing, so under a cap every retry, an immediate one too, travels as a copy. The runtime settles the delivery and publishes a copy of the message back to the queue. The copy carries RETRY_COUNT_HEADER (x-ruststream-retry-count) raised by one, and the handler reads it like any other header. The copy goes back under the queue's own name: on the default exchange a routing key addresses the queue of that name. The delivery that reaches the cap is published under name instead, so name is the queue the message lands in, with its count. A bare queue name, #[subscriber("payments")], takes the same cap. The copies leave through the broker's default publish policy. out_retry(policy) names another one, and the position takes a slot's steps: .codec(..), .transform(..), .to(name). The example names the confirms policy, whose publish resolves once the broker has confirmed the copy. A retry policy aimed at a topic or direct exchange reaches the queue only through a binding under the queue's name. On a quorum queue the same two steps become the queue's own delivery limit.

A declined card is retried at once. The third delivery is the last: the payment goes to payments.dead, where a second subscription reads the count. Macros Manual examples/lapin_settlement_retries.rs /// A card the gateway declines is asked for again, at once. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("payments"))] async fn charge(payment: &Payment) -> HandlerOutcome { if payment.card.starts_with("0000") { tracing::warn!(payment.id, "card declined, retrying"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The payments that ran out of deliveries, with the count the runtime kept. #[subscriber("payments.dead")] async fn bury(payment: &Payment, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { let deliveries = ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("1"); tracing::error!(payment.id, deliveries, "payment dead-lettered"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // Three deliveries, the first included, then the payment goes to `payments.dead`. The // copies leave through the confirms policy, which waits for the broker to confirm each. b.include(charge) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("payments.dead") .out_retry(TransactionalPublish::default()); b.include(bury); }) } examples/manual/lapin_settlement_retries.rs /// A card the gateway declines is asked for again, at once. struct Charge; impl Handle<Payment> for Charge { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if payment.card.starts_with("0000") { tracing::warn!(payment.id, "card declined, retrying"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry())); } ready(Ok(())) } } /// The payments that ran out of deliveries, with the count the runtime kept. struct Bury; impl Handle<Payment> for Bury { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let deliveries = ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("1"); tracing::error!(payment.id, deliveries, "payment dead-lettered"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // Three deliveries, the first included, then the payment goes to `payments.dead`. The // copies leave through the confirms policy, which waits for the broker to confirm each. b.include(subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("payments"), Charge).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("payments.dead") .out_retry(TransactionalPublish::default()); b.include(subscriber("payments.dead", Bury).build()); }) }

retry_after(delay) asks for a redelivery no sooner than delay, for a message that is not ready yet. AMQP has no per-message delay, so on a queue without a delay the runtime waits. It settles the delivery, holds a copy in the service and publishes it back to the queue when the delay is up. The copy goes out under the queue's name on the default exchange, which addresses the queue of that name. It carries RETRY_COUNT_HEADER raised by one. The copy lives in the service's memory, so it is at-most-once over the delay: a process that stops before the timer fires loses it. A retry cap counts these copies like immediate ones.

The first delivery finds the payment unsettled and asks for the refund again in 30 seconds. The copy comes back with the retry count, and the refund goes through. Macros Manual examples/lapin_settlement_retry_after.rs /// The first delivery finds the payment unsettled and asks for the refund again in 30 seconds. /// The copy that comes back carries the retry count, and the refund goes through. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("refunds"))] async fn issue_refund(refund: &Refund, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { if ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).is_none() { tracing::info!(refund.id, "payment not settled yet"); return HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK); } tracing::info!(refund.id, "refunded"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("refunds", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(issue_refund); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_settlement_retry_after.rs /// The first delivery finds the payment unsettled and asks for the refund again in 30 seconds. /// The copy that comes back carries the retry count, and the refund goes through. struct IssueRefund; impl Handle<Refund> for IssueRefund { fn handle( &self, refund: &Refund, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).is_none() { tracing::info!(refund.id, "payment not settled yet"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK))); } tracing::info!(refund.id, "refunded"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("refunds", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("refunds"), IssueRefund).build()); }, ) }

A queue name in #[subscriber] consumes that existing queue as a classic queue; a descriptor carries every other setting. One subscription consumes one queue. #[subscriber("orders")] consumes the queue orders with the defaults of RabbitQueue: a durable classic queue, the broker's prefetch and no bindings. The queue has to exist on the server, unless the broker declares the topology. A message reaches it through the default exchange, which routes on the queue's name, or through an exchange the queue is bound to. RabbitMQ has two queue types, and the type is fixed when the queue is created. The type decides what a retry does, so each type has a descriptor of its own: Descriptor Queue A retry is RabbitQueue classic, on one node counted by the runtime, on the copies it publishes back RabbitQuorumQueue quorum, replicated counted by the server, which ends a message that spent its deliveries A descriptor goes where the name goes, as the attribute's first argument, and every one of its steps returns the descriptor. The manual form passes the name or the descriptor to subscriber(source, body). Several instances of a service share one queue, and each message goes to one of them. The handler's outcome is a protocol frame: an ack removes the message, and a retry or a drop rejects it, as the Settlement pages show. With automatic recovery enabled, a subscription waits while Lapin restores its channel and consumer, then resumes through the same handle. Unsettled deliveries may be redelivered after an outage, so handlers must tolerate duplicates. When retries run out, the stream yields a consume error and ends. Recovery is disabled by default.

An order with items is acknowledged; an empty order is dropped. Macros Manual examples/lapin_subscriptions_queue.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; #[subscriber("orders")] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.items == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "empty order dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.items, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(place); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_subscriptions_queue.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if order.items == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "empty order dropped"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.items, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Place).build()); }, ) }

argument and arguments pass any x- declaration argument the descriptor does not model, such as a TTL or a length limit, verbatim. A queue declaration carries a table of arguments, and RabbitMQ reads queue features from it: x-message-ttl, x-max-length, x-overflow, x-single-active-consumer and more. argument(name, value) adds one entry, and arguments(table) replaces the whole table. The value is an AMQPValue and the table a FieldTable, both re-exported from lapin. A name is at most 255 bytes, the protocol's limit for a field name. The settings the descriptor models, such as the dead-letter exchange and the queue type, travel in the same table, so they are written with their own steps. The arguments reach the server in the queue's declaration, so they take effect where the broker declares the topology. A queue keeps the arguments it was first declared with. A declaration with other arguments is refused with PRECONDITION_FAILED, and startup fails with AmqpError::Declare; the in-process transport refuses it the same way. What an argument does to the messages, such as a TTL that expires them, is the server's work and shows only against a server.

Notifications expire after a minute, and the queue holds at most ten thousand of them. The macro form adds the arguments one by one; the manual form builds the table. Macros Manual examples/lapin_subscriptions_arguments.rs /// A notification older than a minute is no longer worth sending, and the queue keeps at most /// ten thousand of them. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("notifications") .argument("x-message-ttl", AMQPValue::LongLongInt(60_000)) .argument("x-max-length", AMQPValue::LongLongInt(10_000)))] async fn notify(notification: &Notification) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(notification.user, "notification sent"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/lapin_subscriptions_arguments.rs struct Notify; impl Handle<Notification> for Notify { fn handle( &self, notification: &Notification, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(notification.user, "notification sent"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// A notification older than a minute is no longer worth sending, and the queue keeps at most /// ten thousand of them. fn notifications() -> RabbitQueue { let mut arguments = FieldTable::default(); arguments.insert("x-message-ttl".into(), AMQPValue::LongLongInt(60_000)); arguments.insert("x-max-length".into(), AMQPValue::LongLongInt(10_000)); RabbitQueue::new("notifications").arguments(arguments) }

A slice handler gets a batch assembled on the client, up to the mount site's size or until batch_wait (50 ms) passes since the first delivery. A handler over &[T] is a batch handler, and batch(n) at the mount site is its largest batch. AMQP pushes one delivery at a time, so the subscription collects deliveries into a batch on the client. A batch closes when it holds n deliveries, or when batch_wait has passed since its first delivery, 50 ms by default. A raised wait gives fuller batches on a sparse queue; a lowered one hands a short batch over sooner. The server sends no more than the prefetch window, so a window below n keeps every batch below n. One outcome settles every delivery of the batch. In the manual form the body is an impl Handle<[T]>: Ok(()) acknowledges the batch, and Err(outcomes) settles delivery i with outcome i. workers(n) keeps up to n batches in flight at once.

Payments settle up to 32 at a time, and a batch that does not fill closes 200 ms after its first payment. Macros Manual examples/lapin_subscriptions_batches.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; /// Settles up to 32 payments in one call; a batch that does not fill closes 200 ms after its /// first payment arrived. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("payments") .prefetch(nonzero!(64)) .batch_wait(Duration::from_millis(200)))] async fn settle(payments: &[Payment]) -> HandlerOutcome { let cents: u64 = payments.iter().map(|payment| payment.cents).sum(); tracing::info!(count = payments.len(), cents, "payments settled"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(settle.batch(nonzero!(32))); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_subscriptions_batches.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; /// Settles a batch of payments; `Ok` acknowledges the whole batch. struct Settle; impl Handle<[Payment]> for Settle { fn handle( &self, payments: &[Payment], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { let cents: u64 = payments.iter().map(|payment| payment.cents).sum(); tracing::info!(count = payments.len(), cents, "payments settled"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { // Up to 32 payments per call; a batch that does not fill closes 200 ms after its // first payment arrived. let payments = RabbitQueue::new("payments") .prefetch(nonzero!(64)) .batch_wait(Duration::from_millis(200)); b.include(subscriber(payments, Settle).batch(nonzero!(32)).build()); }, ) }

workers(n, by_key) keeps deliveries that share the amqp-partition-key header on one lane, in order, while other keys run in parallel. workers(n, by_key) runs n sequential lanes over one queue. The lane of a delivery is picked by a hash of its partition key, so deliveries with one key run one after another, in queue order. Deliveries with different keys run at once on different lanes. A delivery without a key goes to the next lane in rotation. On RabbitMQ the key is the header PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, amqp-partition-key. AMQP gives the header no meaning: it is a convention between the publisher, which sets it, and this crate, which reads it back. A service that publishes to a keyed queue sets the header on each message, such as the tenant or the account the message belongs to. The lanes order work inside one service instance. Spreading a stream over several queues by key is the consistent-hash exchange, which the server runs. The manual form writes the lanes as .workers_by_key(n) on the mount chain.

Orders of one tenant run in order on one lane, and different tenants run side by side. prefetch caps unacknowledged deliveries per subscription on the broker or one descriptor; unset, the server applies no limit. The server pushes deliveries to a consumer without waiting to be asked. The prefetch window (basic.qos) is how many deliveries it may have out to one subscription before the service settles some of them. So the window is the back-pressure between a queue and a service: a slow handler holds the rest of the queue on the server, where other instances can take it. LapinBroker::prefetch sets the window for every subscription of the broker. RabbitQueue::prefetch and RabbitQuorumQueue::prefetch set it for one subscription and take precedence. The count is a NonZeroU16, because AMQP reads a window of 0 as no limit. A subscription with neither setting has no window, and the server pushes it the whole queue. A batch handler needs a window of at least its batch size, or its batches stay short. The window is the server's: the in-process transport has none and hands a subscription everything its queue holds. A test of the window runs against a server with TestApp::start_live.

RabbitQueue consumes a classic queue: its durability, exclusivity, auto-delete, bindings and the settings shared with quorum queues. RabbitQueue::new names the queue. Three settings belong to the classic queue alone: Setting Default What it does durable true the queue survives a broker restart exclusive false the queue belongs to the connection that declared it and goes with it auto_delete false the server deletes the queue once its last consumer leaves RabbitMQ 4 refuses a transient queue that other connections may share, so durable(false) comes with exclusive(true). An exclusive queue suits a per-instance feed, such as a cache that every instance refreshes from a fanout exchange. The other settings are shared with RabbitQuorumQueue: bind and bind_with join the queue to exchanges, dead_letter_exchange and dead_letter_routing_key give it a route for rejected messages, prefetch and batch_wait shape its consumption, delay parks delayed retries on the server, and argument passes anything else the queue declaration takes. Bindings, the dead-letter route and the arguments reach the server when the broker declares the topology. A classic queue keeps no count of a message's deliveries. A retry puts the message back on the queue, and its next delivery carries the redelivered flag, which a handler reads through the Redelivered key.

The order queue is bound to a topic exchange and dead-letters to orders.failed; an order that fails once is placed on its redelivery. The price queue belongs to this instance alone. Macros Manual examples/lapin_subscriptions_rabbit_queue.rs /// A durable queue fed by the topic exchange `events`; a dropped order leaves through /// `orders.failed`. A delivery the server already handed out once is placed on its second try. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders") .bind(RabbitExchange::topic("events"), "order.*") .dead_letter_exchange("orders.failed"))] async fn place(order: &Order, Ctx(redelivered): Ctx<Redelivered>) -> HandlerOutcome { if !redelivered && order.flaky { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(order.id, redelivered, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// A queue of this instance alone: it lives as long as the connection that declared it. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("prices.instance-a") .durable(false) .exclusive(true) .auto_delete(true) .bind(RabbitExchange::fanout("prices"), ""))] async fn refresh(price: &Price) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(price.sku, price.cents, "price cached"); if !redelivered && order.flaky { return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry())); } tracing::info!(order.id, redelivered, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// A durable queue fed by the topic exchange `events`; a dropped order leaves through /// `orders.failed`. fn orders() -> RabbitQueue { RabbitQueue::new("orders") .bind(RabbitExchange::topic("events"), "order.*") .dead_letter_exchange("orders.failed") } struct Refresh; ready(Ok(())) } } /// A queue of this instance alone: it lives as long as the connection that declared it. fn prices() -> RabbitQueue { RabbitQueue::new("prices.instance-a") .durable(false) .exclusive(true) .auto_delete(true) .bind(RabbitExchange::fanout("prices"), "") }

RabbitQuorumQueue consumes a replicated quorum queue, which is always durable and counts the deliveries each message spends. A quorum queue keeps its messages on several nodes through Raft, so it survives the loss of a node. It is durable, shared and permanent by definition. So the descriptor has no durable, exclusive or auto_delete step, and a quorum queue that contradicts its type does not compile. Every shared setting of RabbitQueue is on it too. The server counts each delivery of a message, and a retry spends one. A quorum delivery reports its count, where a classic delivery reports only the redelivered flag. Past the queue's delivery limit the server takes the message off the queue: it dead-letters the message when the queue has a dead-letter exchange, and drops it otherwise. RabbitMQ 4 gives a quorum queue a limit of 20 when it names none, so a message that keeps failing gets 21 deliveries. delivery_limit sets another limit; max_attempts with dead_letter at the mount site sets it from the registration. The queue type is part of the declaration, so a quorum queue is created by an operator or by a broker that declares the topology. A quorum queue refuses some classic arguments: a declaration with x-max-priority fails with AmqpError::Declare.

A reservation waits for stock; one that never fits ends after the queue's default delivery limit. Macros Manual examples/lapin_subscriptions_quorum.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; /// A reservation waits for stock; the queue gives up on one after its delivery limit. #[subscriber(RabbitQuorumQueue::new("reservations"))] async fn reserve(reservation: &Reservation) -> HandlerOutcome { if !reservation.in_stock { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(reservation.id, "reserved"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("reservations", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(reserve); }) } examples/manual/lapin_subscriptions_quorum.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; /// A reservation waits for stock; the queue gives up on one after its delivery limit. struct Reserve; impl Handle<Reservation> for Reserve { fn handle( &self, reservation: &Reservation, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if !reservation.in_stock { return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry())); } tracing::info!(reservation.id, "reserved"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("reservations", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let reservations = RabbitQuorumQueue::new("reservations"); b.include(subscriber(reservations, Reserve).build()); }) }

TestApp::start runs the production app on LapinBroker in process, with exchanges, bindings, requeues, quorum counts and reply-to. A test hands the harness the app main runs, unchanged, and addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<LapinBroker>(). The testing feature in [dev-dependencies] adds the in-process mode, and turns on the core's harness with it. The in-process transport has no settings of its own. It reads the broker's: declare_topology decides whether a subscription declares its queue, as on the server. A publish is framed by the same conversion a publish to the server goes through. The transport keeps RabbitMQ's semantics. The default exchange and the direct, topic, fanout and headers exchanges route through the bindings the descriptors declare. Consumers of one queue compete for its messages, and a requeue puts a message back in its queue. A queue keeps what reaches it from its first subscription on, until an auto-delete queue loses its last consumer. A consumer that closes returns what it took and left unsettled. A quorum queue counts deliveries and dead-letters a spent one through its route. A waiting queue releases a delayed copy, and direct reply-to gives every request an address of its own. The transport refuses what the server refuses, with the same error. That covers a name over 255 bytes, a header the frame cannot carry, and a body over the server's default max_message_size of 16 MiB. It covers the declarations the server refuses: a transient queue that is not exclusive, a binding on the default exchange, a queue declared again with other settings, a quorum queue with a priority. A delivery settled after its connection closed reports the closed channel. A publish through the harness returns once every handler it woke has settled, a reply or a slot publish included. The assertions that follow read finished state. What only a server has is for a live test: the prefetch window, publisher confirms, the atomicity of a server transaction, a plugin exchange's routing, a queue two connections share, and a topology the service finds without declaring it.

TestApp::start_live runs the same test body against a running RabbitMQ, one subscription per queue, for what only a server has. It connects the broker through its ordinary connect, so every subscription consumes from the server. The body is the one an in-process test runs; only the start call differs. A publish, settle and advance wait on the real clock until every subscription has handled what was published to it. The wait lasts ten seconds at most, and start_live_within sets another bound. The live mode is for what the in-process transport leaves to the server: the prefetch window, publisher confirms, the atomicity of a server transaction, a plugin exchange's routing, and a topology the service finds without declaring it. A live test keeps one subscription per queue. The server picks which consumer of a queue takes a message, so a test with two subscriptions of one queue stops at the first publish and names the queue. A server keeps what earlier runs left in it. In the example the service declares its queue with declare_topology, and the queue is exclusive: it lives as long as the test's connection. live::url is the repository's test helper: it returns the server's address from AMQP_TEST_URL, and the test returns early without one, so cargo test passes on a machine with no server. A job that stood a server up sets RUSTSTREAM_REQUIRE_LIVE=1, and a missing address then fails the test instead of skipping it. The repository's stand is docker-compose.test.yml, which just brokers-up starts.

The two tests share one body: one in process, one against the server at AMQP_TEST_URL. A handler bounded Out<impl TransactionalPublisher> opens a transaction scope with begin, publishes through it, and ends it with commit or abort. The scope's publishes become visible together at commit, and abort discards them. The handler names the capability, TransactionalPublisher, and the mount site names the policy that provides it. ConfirmsPublish, TransactionalPublish in the prelude, buffers in the client and commits by awaiting a broker confirm for every message. ServerTxPublish runs an AMQP channel transaction on the server. LapinPublish pairs into a publisher with no transaction surface, so a transactional handler mounted with it does not compile. A publisher runs one such transaction at a time. A second begin while one is open, or a commit or abort with none open, fails with AmqpError::Transaction and leaves the open transaction as it was. A publisher is a shared handle: every clone uses one channel and one transaction state. Several independent groups of messages in one handler take the owned kind, ConfirmsTransaction.

An order ships one message per item, in one transaction. An item without a name aborts the transaction, and the shipments already published are discarded. Macros Manual examples/lapin_transactions_scope.rs /// One shipment per item, in one transaction. An item without a name aborts it, and the shipments /// already published are discarded with it. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"))] async fn ship(order: &Order, Out(shipments): Out<impl TransactionalPublisher>) -> HandlerOutcome { let Ok(scope) = shipments.begin().await else { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); }; for item in &order.items { if item.is_empty() { tracing::warn!(order.id, "an item without a name, nothing shipped"); return match scope.abort().await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::drop(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), }; } let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id, item: item.clone(), }; if scope.message(&shipment).publish().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } } if scope.commit().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/lapin_transactions_scope.rs /// One shipment per item, in one transaction. An item without a name aborts it, and the shipments /// already published are discarded with it. struct Ship; impl<Egress> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Egress,)>> for Ship where Egress: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: TransactionalPublisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Egress,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let scope = outs .get(DefaultSlot) .begin() .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry())?; for item in &order.items { if item.is_empty() { tracing::warn!(order.id, "an item without a name, nothing shipped"); scope.abort().await.map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry())?; return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id, item: item.clone(), }; if scope.message(&shipment).publish().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } } scope.commit().await.map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } Macros Manual examples/lapin_transactions_scope.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { // The confirms policy; `LapinPublish::default().server_tx()` is the other one. b.include(ship) .out(DefaultSlot, TransactionalPublish::default()) .build(); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_transactions_scope.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { // The confirms policy; `LapinPublish::default().server_tx()` is the other one. b.include(subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"), Ship).build()) .out(DefaultSlot, TransactionalPublish::default()) .build(); }, ) }

ConfirmsPublish, TransactionalPublish in the prelude, is the publish policy whose every publish resolves once the broker has confirmed the message. LapinPublish::confirms reaches it with the same settings: exchange and property defaults. It pairs into a ConfirmsPublisher with a confirm channel of its own. A message the broker refuses fails the publish, and the handler decides what follows. RabbitMQ confirms a message once it has routed it, and a message that matches no queue is confirmed and dropped. So a confirm says the broker took the message, not that a queue holds it. Inside a transaction the publisher buffers in the client. commit publishes the buffer in order and resolves once every message is confirmed, and abort discards the buffer without touching the broker. A failed commit loses the buffer, and the delivery's redelivery is the way to recover. The policy offers the borrowed kind of the transaction scope and the owned kind of ConfirmsTransaction.

A payment is acknowledged once the broker has confirmed its receipt. A receipt the broker refused brings the payment back. Macros Manual examples/lapin_transactions_confirms.rs /// The payment is acknowledged once the broker has confirmed its receipt. A receipt the broker /// refused brings the payment back. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("payments"))] async fn settle(payment: &Payment, Out(receipts): Out<impl Publisher>) -> HandlerOutcome { let receipt = Receipt { payment_id: payment.id, }; if let Err(err) = receipts.message(&receipt).publish().await { tracing::warn!(payment.id, %err, "receipt not confirmed"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(payment.id, payment.cents, "payment settled"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(settle) .out(DefaultSlot, TransactionalPublish::default()) .build(); }) } examples/manual/lapin_transactions_confirms.rs /// The payment is acknowledged once the broker has confirmed its receipt. A receipt the broker /// refused brings the payment back. struct Settle; impl<Egress> Handle<Payment, (), Outs<(Egress,)>> for Settle where Egress: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, outs: &Outs<(Egress,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let receipt = Receipt { payment_id: payment.id, }; let receipts = outs.get(DefaultSlot); if let Err(err) = receipts.message(&receipt).publish().await { tracing::warn!(payment.id, %err, "receipt not confirmed"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } tracing::info!(payment.id, payment.cents, "payment settled"); Ok(()) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("payments"), Settle).build()) .out(DefaultSlot, TransactionalPublish::default()) .build(); }) }

ConfirmsTransaction is an owned confirm transaction: a value that holds its own publish buffer. A handler bounded Out<impl OwnedTransactions, Slot> opens one with transaction() on its slot, and every call opens another. Any number can be open on one publisher, and settling one never touches another. The publisher keeps publishing directly while they are open. commit publishes the buffer in order and awaits every confirm, and abort discards it without touching the broker. Both consume the value, so a double commit or a publish after settling does not compile. A failed commit loses the buffer, and the delivery's redelivery is the way to recover. Only ConfirmsPublish offers the owned kind.

The shipment and the audit record of an order go out in two transactions. An order out of stock aborts the shipment and still commits its audit record. Macros Manual examples/lapin_transactions_owned.rs #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Shipment, AuditRecord)] struct Records; /// The shipment and the audit record go out in two transactions. The shipment waits in its own /// buffer while the stock is checked: an order out of stock aborts it and still commits its audit /// record. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"))] async fn record( order: &Order, Out(records): Out<impl OwnedTransactions, Records>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let (Ok(mut shipment), Ok(mut audit)) = (records.transaction().await, records.transaction().await) else { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); }; let shipped = Shipment { order_id: order.id }; if shipment.message(&shipped).publish().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } let settled = if order.in_stock { shipment.commit().await } else { shipment.abort().await }; if settled.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } let entry = AuditRecord { order_id: order.id, shipped: order.in_stock, }; if audit.message(&entry).publish().await.is_err() || audit.commit().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(record) .out(Records, TransactionalPublish::default()) .build(); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_transactions_owned.rs #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Shipment, AuditRecord)] struct Records; /// The shipment and the audit record go out in two transactions. ServerTxPublish is the publish policy backed by AMQP channel transactions: tx.select, tx.commit and tx.rollback. LapinPublish::server_tx reaches it with the same settings. It pairs into a ServerTxPublisher on a channel of its own. Between begin and commit the messages wait on the broker inside the channel transaction, and they become visible together at commit. abort rolls them back on the server. Each commit is a synchronous round trip, which makes the policy slower than ConfirmsPublish. Outside a transaction a publish behaves like a fire-and-forget one. The transaction is the channel's state, so the policy offers only the borrowed kind of the transaction scope. Server transactions require auto_recover(false), which is the default. Lapin cannot restore a transaction's state after a disconnect, so pairing this policy with auto_recover(true) fails with AmqpError::InvalidOptions before it is used. Direct publish, begin, commit and abort calls also reject that combination. Use publisher confirms when enabling connection recovery.

Cargo.toml [dependencies] ruststream = { version = "0.7", features = ["macros", "json", "asyncapi", "logging"] } ruststream-lapin = "0.7" serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] } tracing = "0.1" [dev-dependencies] ruststream-lapin = { version = "0.7", features = ["testing"] } tokio = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt"] } ruststream is the framework: macros gives the attributes, json the default codec, asyncapi the service's AsyncAPI document, and logging prints the service's log to the terminal. ruststream-lapin is the RabbitMQ broker, built on lapin, an AMQP 0.9.1 client written in Rust. The build needs nothing outside Cargo. Its testing feature adds the in-process RabbitMQ that tests run on. The broker crate has these features: Feature What it gives asyncapi the AMQP bindings in the generated AsyncAPI document testing the in-process RabbitMQ behind TestApp tls-native-tls TLS through the platform's TLS library tls-rustls TLS through rustls tls-rustls-ring TLS through rustls with the ring crypto provider plugin-consistent-hash the consistent-hash exchange of the RabbitMQ plugin plugin-dme a delayed retry through the delayed-message-exchange plugin

One RabbitMQ node with the management UI is enough to develop against: compose.yaml services: rabbitmq: image: rabbitmq:4-management-alpine ports: - "127.0.0.1:5672:5672" - "127.0.0.1:15672:15672" docker compose up -d The broker listens on localhost:5672. The management UI is at http://localhost:15672, user guest, password guest. RabbitMQ accepts the guest account only from localhost, which is how the ports are published.

This guide configures the connection of a RabbitMQ service for production and describes what it does when the connection or the service goes away.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// The broker as production runs it. fn broker(uri: String) -> LapinBroker { LapinBroker::new(uri) // What the management UI lists for this service's connection. .connection_name(concat!("orders ", env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"))) // At most 64 unacknowledged deliveries per subscription. .prefetch(nonzero!(64)) } fn service(broker: LapinBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(take_order); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { // amqps://orders:secret@rabbit.internal:5671/shop in production. let uri = env::var("AMQP_URL").unwrap_or_else(|_| "amqp://localhost:5672".to_owned()); service(broker(uri)) } src/main.rs /// The broker as production runs it. fn broker(uri: String) -> LapinBroker { LapinBroker::new(uri) // What the management UI lists for this service's connection. .connection_name(concat!("orders ", env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"))) // At most 64 unacknowledged deliveries per subscription. .prefetch(nonzero!(64)) } fn service(broker: LapinBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"), TakeOrder).build()); }) } fn app() -> RustStream { // amqps://orders:secret@rabbit.internal:5671/shop in production. let uri = env::var("AMQP_URL").unwrap_or_else(|_| "amqp://localhost:5672".to_owned()); service(broker(uri)) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } The connection URI carries everything about the connection: the scheme, the credentials, the host, the port and the virtual host. amqp://orders:secret@rabbit.internal:5672/shop logs in as orders to the virtual host shop. The default virtual host / is written %2f. RabbitMQ's URI specification lists the query parameters, such as heartbeat. The service reads the URI from AMQP_URL, so the secret stays out of the code. connection_name labels the connection in the management UI, so an operator sees which service and version holds it. prefetch caps the unacknowledged deliveries of each subscription, which is how a slow service pushes back on the server (Work queues). LapinBroker::new only records the URI. The service connects at startup, and a URI it cannot parse or a server it cannot reach stops the start with AmqpError::Connect.

An amqps:// URI connects over TLS, usually on port 5671. TLS comes from one of three features of ruststream-lapin, each mapped onto lapin's own: Feature TLS library tls-native-tls the platform's: OpenSSL on Linux, Secure Transport on macOS, SChannel on Windows tls-rustls rustls tls-rustls-ring rustls with the ring crypto provider The server's certificate is checked against the trusted roots of the chosen library. RabbitMQ's TLS guide covers the server side. The TLS component shows the dependency lines. The service's AsyncAPI document reports the host and the AMQP version, never the credentials or the virtual host of the URI: the document is published and shared.

A production service usually runs with declare_topology off, against queues that operations create and change. A queue that does not exist then fails the start instead of losing messages (Topology). A quorum queue's attempt cap and a delayed retry's waiting queue are the server's in that setup too (Acknowledgements, retries and dead letters).

One connection carries the whole service. Each subscription opens a channel of its own, so an error on one queue does not stop the others. Fire-and-forget publishes share one channel. A confirms publisher, a channel-transaction publisher and a requester each open a channel of their own on first use, because confirms, transactions and direct reply-to are the state of a channel. RabbitMQ closes a channel on a channel-level error, such as a publish to an exchange that does not exist. The connection stays up, and a publisher opens a new channel on its next call.

Connection recovery is disabled by default. Enable LapinBroker::auto_recover(true) to let Lapin reconnect with exponential backoff, including the initial connection. The default limit is 16 retries; .recovery_retries(n) changes it, and zero disables retries. Lapin restores channels, declared exchanges, queues, bindings, prefetch, publisher confirms and consumers through the existing handles. It does not restart the application or rerun startup hooks. Configure a heartbeat in the URI, such as amqp://localhost:5672?heartbeat=30, to detect silent connection loss. ConnectedLapinBroker::is_connected() checks the AMQP connection for a readiness endpoint: false during disconnection or after shutdown. A true result does not mean channel and topology recovery has finished or that workers are healthy; it is separate from the service's runtime health. Failed publishes are not replayed, and deadlines of RPC requests in flight keep running. ServerTxPublish requires auto_recover(false) because transaction state is lost on reconnect. If retries run out at startup, connection fails; after startup, the consumer stream yields a terminal consume error and ends. Unsettled deliveries in queues that survive the disconnect return to RabbitMQ and can be redelivered, marked Redelivered. Handlers must tolerate duplicates. A consumer cancelled by the server on a live channel, such as after its queue is deleted, ends its subscription.

SIGTERM or Ctrl+C stops the service. The runtime stops the subscriptions and closes the connection with a clean handshake. RabbitMQ returns every delivery the service took and did not settle to its queue, so another instance takes it. A publisher or a requester that outlives the connection, for example one held by a background task, returns AmqpError::Closed instead of sending into a closed connection. If shutdown begins during reconnect, waiting consumers are woken and broker shutdown does not wait for RabbitMQ to return. Existing handles are closed immediately; a later recovered connection is closed in the background, or cleanup ends when retries run out.

The tests in the example file start the service from an amqps:// URI with credentials and from a malformed one. In process, the URI is parsed as a connection parses it, so a URI the service could not connect with does not start a test either. TLS and connection loss need a server, so they belong to a live test.

This guide chooses how sure a service is that RabbitMQ took its messages, and sets the properties of one message. The guarantee is a property of the publish policy at the mount site, not a flag on each call: Policy Prelude name A publish resolves when LapinPublish Publish the frame is written to the connection ConfirmsPublish TransactionalPublish RabbitMQ confirmed the message ServerTxPublish ServerTxPublish the channel transaction commits The example is an orders service. It turns an order into one shipment per parcel, all of them or none, and books a courier for each shipment, an expedited one ahead of the rest.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] struct Order { id: u64, parcels: Vec<String>, expedited: bool, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "shipments")] struct Shipment { order_id: u64, parcel: String, expedited: bool, } /// Publishes one shipment per parcel: every one of them, or none. async fn ship_all( shipments: &impl TransactionalPublisher, order: &Order, ) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> { let scope = shipments.begin().await?; for parcel in &order.parcels { if parcel.is_empty() { scope.abort().await?; return Err("a parcel without a description".into()); } let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id, parcel: parcel.clone(), expedited: order.expedited, }; scope.message(&shipment).publish().await?; } // Resolves once RabbitMQ confirmed every shipment of the order. scope.commit().await?; Ok(()) } #[subscriber("orders")] async fn pack_order( order: &Order, Out(shipments): Out<impl TransactionalPublisher>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { match ship_all(shipments, order).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(order.id, %err, "order not shipped"); HandlerOutcome::drop() } } } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Order { id: u64, parcels: Vec<String>, expedited: bool, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] #[outgoing(name = "shipments")] struct Shipment { order_id: u64, parcel: String, expedited: bool, } /// Publishes one shipment per parcel: every one of them, or none. async fn ship_all( shipments: &impl TransactionalPublisher, order: &Order, ) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> { let scope = shipments.begin().await?; for parcel in &order.parcels { if parcel.is_empty() { scope.abort().await?; return Err("a parcel without a description".into()); } let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id, parcel: parcel.clone(), expedited: order.expedited, }; scope.message(&shipment).publish().await?; } // Resolves once RabbitMQ confirmed every shipment of the order. scope.commit().await?; Ok(()) } struct PackOrder; impl<Shipments> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Shipments,)>> for PackOrder where Shipments: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: TransactionalPublisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Shipments,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { ship_all(outs.get(DefaultSlot), order).await.map_err(|err| { tracing::warn!(order.id, %err, "order not shipped"); HandlerOutcome::drop() }) } } pack_order bounds its slot Out<impl TransactionalPublisher>, so it mounts only on a policy with transactions. begin opens a scope, and every shipment published in it waits in the service. commit publishes them and resolves once RabbitMQ has confirmed each one. A parcel without a description aborts the scope, and no shipment of that order leaves. A commit that fails returns an error, and the order can be delivered again and packed again. RabbitMQ confirms a message once it has taken responsibility for it: written to disk for a persistent message on a durable queue, accepted by a quorum queue's majority. RabbitMQ's confirms guide describes when each message is confirmed. A confirm does not mean a queue received the message. RabbitMQ confirms a message that matches no binding and drops it, because the crate publishes without the mandatory flag. So a confirmed publish goes to an exchange whose bindings exist, or to a queue that exists: declare them with the service (Topology), or check them where operations own them.

ServerTxPublish, reached with Publish::default().server_tx(), uses AMQP channel transactions instead. The messages of a transaction become visible together at commit, which is a synchronous round trip to the server. Confirms are faster and cover most cases. Take a channel transaction when the consumers must never see half of a group, for example both legs of a transfer. A handler bounded Out<impl TransactionalPublisher> mounts on either policy unchanged. A ConfirmsTransaction, opened with owned_transaction, owns its buffer instead of borrowing the publisher: several can be open at once, and each commits on its own. Channel transactions offer only the borrowed scope, because the transaction is the state of the channel itself.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "pickups")] struct Pickup { order_id: u64, parcel: String, } /// The slot pickups leave through. #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Pickup)] struct Pickups;
