let sent = if shipment.expedited { pickups .message(&pickup) .priority(9) .expiration(Duration::from_hours(1)) .publish() .await } else { pickups.message(&pickup).publish().await }; if sent.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] #[outgoing(name = "pickups")] struct Pickup { order_id: u64, parcel: String, } /// The slot pickups leave through. #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Pickup)] struct Pickups; /// An expedited pickup jumps the couriers' queue and is worthless after an hour. struct BookCourier; impl<Couriers> Handle<Shipment, (), Outs<(Couriers,)>> for BookCourier where Couriers: OutEntry<Pickups, Wire: Publisher<Options = LapinPublishOptions>>, { async fn handle( &self, shipment: &Shipment, outs: &Outs<(Couriers,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let pickups = outs.get(Pickups); let pickup = Pickup { order_id: shipment.order_id, parcel: shipment.parcel.clone(), }; let sent = if shipment.expedited { pickups .message(&pickup) .priority(9) .expiration(Duration::from_hours(1)) .publish() .await } else { pickups.message(&pickup).publish().await }; sent.map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } AMQP gives each message three properties of its own: the priority, the expiration and the delivery mode. The policy sets what every message through it carries, here priority 3. The publish builder's steps set them for one message: an expedited pickup goes out at priority 9 and expires after an hour unread. The slot is bounded on LapinPublishOptions, so the handler names no publisher type; the steps come from the crate's prelude. None of the three travels as a header: each is an AMQP property, where RabbitMQ reads it. A delivery reports them back as headers, under PRIORITY_HEADER and EXPIRATION_HEADER. A priority orders deliveries only on a queue declared with x-max-priority; on any other queue RabbitMQ ignores it. The couriers' pickups queue is declared with that argument by whoever owns it. Every policy publishes persistent messages unless persistent(false) says otherwise, so a message on a durable queue survives a broker restart.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // Confirms: a publish resolves once RabbitMQ has taken the message. b.include(pack_order) .out(DefaultSlot, TransactionalPublish::default()) .build(); // Every pickup leaves at priority 3 unless the handler says otherwise. b.include(book_courier) .out(Pickups, Publish::default().priority(3)) .build(); }) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App { let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // Confirms: a publish resolves once RabbitMQ has taken the message. b.include(subscriber("orders", PackOrder).build()) .out(DefaultSlot, TransactionalPublish::default()) .build(); // Every pickup leaves at priority 3 unless the handler says otherwise. b.include(subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("shipments"), BookCourier).build()) .out(Pickups, Publish::default().priority(3)) .build(); }) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } TransactionalPublish::default() is ConfirmsPublish. Publish::default().priority(3) is the plain policy with a priority for every message. .confirms() and .server_tx() move a plain policy to the stronger ones and keep its settings, such as its exchange. Fire-and-forget publishes share one channel of the connection; a confirms or transactional publisher opens a channel of its own, because both modes are channel state. A service publishes outside a handler too, for example from an HTTP endpoint, through a publisher the app hands out at startup (LapinPublish).

The tests in the example file check that an order ships every parcel, that a bad parcel ships none, and which properties each pickup carries, read with tb.out::<Pickups>(). The in-process RabbitMQ buffers a transaction until it commits and frames each message as a server would. What a confirm means and the atomicity of a channel transaction are the server's, so they belong to a live test. Testing a RabbitMQ service covers the harness.

This guide settles RabbitMQ deliveries, retries them now or later, caps the attempts and moves what keeps failing to a dead-letter queue. The example is a refunds service. Refunds arrive on a classic queue, payouts on a quorum queue, and both go to a dead-letter queue after five deliveries.

A handler's outcome becomes an AMQP frame on the delivery's channel: Outcome Frame What RabbitMQ does HandlerOutcome::ack() basic.ack removes the message from the queue HandlerOutcome::retry() basic.reject with requeue puts the message back in the queue HandlerOutcome::drop() basic.reject without requeue removes the message, or dead-letters it where the queue has a dead-letter exchange HandlerOutcome::retry_after(delay) an acknowledged delivery and a delayed copy delivers the copy again once the delay has passed RabbitMQ counts every rejection as a delivery the message has spent. So a handler that keeps asking for its message back runs a quorum queue's own limit down. A delivery the service took and never settled goes back to the queue when the channel or the connection closes.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// How long a busy processor asks its callers to wait. const BACKOFF: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] struct Refund { id: u64, card: String, amount_cents: u64, } /// Refunds wait out a delay in the broker's waiting queue, `refunds.retry`. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("refunds").delay(Delay::dlx_ttl()))] async fn process_refund( refund: &Refund, State(processor): State<Arc<Processor>>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { match processor.refund(&refund.card).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), // Past the rate limit: a delivery right now would be refused again. Err(Refusal::Busy) => HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF), // No answer: try again at once, up to the attempt cap. Err(Refusal::Unavailable) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), Err(Refusal::Declined) => { tracing::warn!(refund.id, "card declined, refund dropped"); HandlerOutcome::drop() } } } src/main.rs /// How long a busy processor asks its callers to wait. const BACKOFF: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Refund { id: u64, card: String, amount_cents: u64, } struct ProcessRefund; impl Handle<Refund, (), (), (), Clients> for ProcessRefund { async fn handle( &self, refund: &Refund, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { match ctx.state().processor.refund(&refund.card).await { Ok(()) => Ok(()), // Past the rate limit: a delivery right now would be refused again. Err(Refusal::Busy) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF)), // No answer: try again at once, up to the attempt cap. Err(Refusal::Unavailable) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()), Err(Refusal::Declined) => { tracing::warn!(refund.id, "card declined, refund dropped"); Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()) } } } } /// Refunds wait out a delay in the broker's waiting queue, `refunds.retry`. fn refunds_queue() -> RabbitQueue { RabbitQueue::new("refunds").delay(Delay::dlx_ttl()) } The card processor refuses a refund in three ways, and each needs a different outcome. Busy means its rate limit is used up: a retry right now would be refused again, so retry_after waits 30 seconds. Unavailable means it did not answer: retry tries again at once. Declined means the card account is closed, and another try gets the same answer, so the refund is dropped.

The fifth delivery is not retried: dead_letter publishes it to refunds.dead. A destination is a routing key on the default exchange, so the refund lands in the queue of that name. A classic queue counts nothing, so the cap is the service's. Under a cap, a retry acknowledges the delivery and publishes a copy back to the queue under its own name. The copy carries the attempt count in the x-ruststream-retry-count header (RETRY_COUNT_HEADER), raised by one. The copies leave through the broker's default publish policy; .out_retry(policy) names another, for example TransactionalPublish to wait for RabbitMQ's confirm of each copy. A dropped refund does not reach refunds.dead: the dead-letter queue holds only the refunds that ran out of attempts. To keep dropped messages too, give the queue its own dead-letter exchange (Topology).

documents.t: Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] struct Payout { id: u64, card: String, amount_cents: u64, } /// Payouts live in a quorum queue, which counts their deliveries itself. #[subscriber(RabbitQuorumQueue::new("payouts"))] async fn send_payout(payout: &Payout, State(processor): State<Arc<Processor>>) -> HandlerOutcome { match processor.refund(&payout.card).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(Refusal::Busy | Refusal::Unavailable) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), Err(Refusal::Declined) => HandlerOutcome::drop(), } } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Payout { id: u64, card: String, amount_cents: u64, } struct SendPayout; impl Handle<Payout, (), (), (), Clients> for SendPayout { async fn handle( &self, payout: &Payout, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { match ctx.state().processor.refund(&payout.card).await { Ok(()) => Ok(()), Err(Refusal::Busy | Refusal::Unavailable) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()), Err(Refusal::Declined) => Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()), } } } /// Payouts live in a quorum queue, which counts their deliveries itself. fn payouts_queue() -> RabbitQuorumQueue { RabbitQuorumQueue::new("payouts") } A quorum queue counts the deliveries of each message itself. On payouts, the same two steps at the mount site become the queue's x-delivery-limit and its dead-letter route. The server then moves a payout to payouts.dead after its fifth delivery, whether or not a service is running, and the service publishes nothing. A retry stays a plain basic.reject with requeue. The arguments reach the queue only where the service declares it, so this needs declare_topology(true). On a broker that declares nothing, the service refuses to start: a queue declared elsewhere carries its owner's arguments, and the cap would apply nowhere. There, set the limit and the route on the queue itself, by its declaration or a policy, and mount the handler without the two steps. Half a declaration is refused too, because a limit with nowhere to send the spent message drops it. .out_retry(..) does not compile on a quorum queue: there is no copy to publish. A quorum queue declared without a limit has RabbitMQ 4's default of 20 deliveries; delivery_limit sets another on the descriptor. A quorum delivery reports how many deliveries it has spent through redelivery_count(). A classic delivery reports only Redelivered, whether RabbitMQ handed it out before.

documents.t: AMQP has no per-message delay. Without a delay on the queue, retry_after holds the copy in the service and publishes it when the delay has passed. That copy is at-most-once: a service that stops during the delay loses it. delay(Delay::dlx_ttl()) moves the wait to RabbitMQ. The copy waits in the queue refunds.retry under a per-message TTL, and the waiting queue dead-letters it back to refunds when the TTL fires. The original is acknowledged after the copy is published on the same channel, so a failure between the two duplicates the refund rather than losing it. The copy is a new message, so it carries the retry count raised by one, and the cap ends a delayed loop as it ends an immediate one. A waiting queue releases messages only from its head. A message with a long delay holds back every message behind it, so mixed delays want one waiting queue per delay, named with Delay::dlx_ttl_named. The plugin-dme feature adds Delay::plugin_dme, which waits in RabbitMQ's delayed-message-exchange plugin, where a short delay never waits behind a long one. The waiting queue and the delayed exchange are infrastructure. Under declare_topology(true) the service declares them. With declaration off, a subscription with a delay checks at startup that its waiting queue or its delayed exchange exists, and the service does not start without it.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber("refunds.dead")] async fn review_refund(refund: &Refund, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { let deliveries = ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("1"); tracing::error!(refund.id, deliveries, "refund needs a person to look at it"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[subscriber("payouts.dead")] async fn review_payout(payout: &Payout) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::error!(payout.id, "payout needs a person to look at it"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs struct ReviewRefund; impl Handle<Refund, (), (), (), Clients> for ReviewRefund { fn handle( &self, refund: &Refund, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let deliveries = ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("1"); tracing::error!(refund.id, deliveries, "refund needs a person to look at it"); ready(Ok(())) } } struct ReviewPayout; impl Handle<Payout, (), (), (), Clients> for ReviewPayout { fn handle( &self, payout: &Payout, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::error!(payout.id, "payout needs a person to look at it"); ready(Ok(())) } } A dead-letter queue is an ordinary queue, and a handler reads it like any other. A refund the service dead-lettered carries the retry-count header with the number of deliveries it went through, 5 here. A payout the quorum queue dead-lettered carries RabbitMQ's own x-death header instead. Both handlers log the message for a person to look at.

The tests in the example file run the app in process with a paused clock, so tb.advance(BACKOFF) lets the 30 seconds pass at once. The in-process RabbitMQ releases the waiting queue's copy, counts a quorum queue's deliveries and dead-letters a spent one through its route, as the server does. The delayed-message-exchange plugin works only on a server, so its tests run against a live RabbitMQ. Testing a RabbitMQ service covers the harness.

This guide routes messages through RabbitMQ exchanges: by routing key, to every bound queue, and by headers. A publisher never writes to a queue. It publishes to an exchange with a routing key, and the exchange copies the message into every queue whose binding matches. In RustStream a queue's bindings are written on its descriptor, and the exchange a message goes to belongs to the publish policy. The routing key is the message's name: the #[outgoing(name = "..")] of its type, or the name the publish gives it. The example is a shop that announces orders on a topic exchange, price changes on a fanout exchange and shipments on a headers exchange. The broker declares the exchanges, the queues and the bindings, so the example runs on an empty RabbitMQ (Topology).

Every service so far published to the default exchange. It is a direct exchange that every queue is bound to under its own name. So a message with the routing key orders reaches the queue orders, and a service reads it with #[subscriber("orders")] and no binding at all. A binding on the default exchange is refused, by the server and by the in-process RabbitMQ alike. A direct exchange of your own routes the same way: a binding names one routing key, and a message reaches the queues bound under exactly its key.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] struct Order { id: u64, region: String, } /// An order event; its routing key is `order.placed.<region>`. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] struct OrderPlaced { id: u64, region: String, } /// Takes an order from the `orders` queue and announces it on the `events` exchange. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn place_order(order: &Order, Out(events): Out<impl Publisher>) -> HandlerOutcome { let placed = OrderPlaced { id: order.id, region: order.region.clone(), }; let key = format!("order.placed.{}", order.region); if events.message(&placed).to(&key).publish().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Every order event of every region. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("notifications.orders") .bind(RabbitExchange::topic("events"), "order.placed.*"))] async fn notify_customer(event: &OrderPlaced, Ctx(key): Ctx<RoutingKey>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(event.id, routing_key = %key, "customer notified"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Every event on the exchange, whatever its key. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("audit").bind(RabbitExchange::topic("events"), "#"))] async fn audit(event: &OrderPlaced, Ctx(key): Ctx<RoutingKey>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(event.id, routing_key = %key, "event audited"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Order { id: u64, region: String, } /// An order event; impl<Events> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Events,)>> for PlaceOrder where Events: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Events,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let placed = OrderPlaced { id: order.id, region: order.region.clone(), }; let key = format!("order.placed.{}", order.region); let sent = outs .get(DefaultSlot) .message(&placed) .to(&key) .publish() .await; sent.map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } /// Every order event of every region. struct NotifyCustomer; impl Handle<OrderPlaced, (), (), AmqpContext> for NotifyCustomer { fn handle( &self, event: &OrderPlaced, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, AmqpContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(event.id, routing_key = %ctx.context(RoutingKey), "customer notified"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// The events of the EU region only. struct ReserveStock; impl Handle<OrderPlaced> for ReserveStock { fn handle( &self, event: &OrderPlaced, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(event.id, "stock reserved in the EU warehouse"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// Every event on the exchange, whatever its key. struct Audit; impl Handle<OrderPlaced, (), (), AmqpContext> for Audit { fn handle( &self, event: &OrderPlaced, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, AmqpContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(event.id, routing_key = %ctx.context(RoutingKey), "event audited"); ready(Ok(())) } } place_order publishes each order as OrderPlaced with the routing key order.placed.<region>. The type declares no name, so the publish names it with .to(&key). A topic exchange matches the key against each binding's pattern, word by word, with dots between the words. * stands for exactly one word and # for any number of words, none included. So order.placed.* takes the orders of every region, *.*.eu only the EU's, and # every message on the exchange. An order from the US reaches the notifications and the audit, and the EU warehouse never sees it. A handler reads the key a message arrived with through Ctx<RoutingKey>.

b.include( subscriber( RabbitQueue::new("insurance").bind_with(shipments, "", gold_in_eu("any")), Insure, ) .build(), ); }) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } The exchange is named once, on the policy at the mount site: Publish::default().exchange("events"). The handler's body names only the message and its key, so the same handler publishes to another exchange when the mount site says so. A reply takes the same policy at .out_reply(..). RabbitMQ refuses a publish to an exchange that does not exist and closes the channel the publish went over. Here the subscriptions declare events, prices and shipments at startup, before any handler publishes. A service that publishes to an exchange it does not read from relies on operations or on another service to declare it. Every binding of a subscription also appears in the service's AsyncAPI document, in the x-ruststream-amqp extension of its channel.

The plugin-consistent-hash feature adds RabbitExchange::consistent_hash, the exchange type of RabbitMQ's consistent hash plugin. It spreads one stream of messages over several queues by a hash of the routing key, and each queue binds with its weight as the routing key. Messages with the same key always reach the same queue. The plugin must be enabled on the server, and the routing happens only there, so its tests run against a live RabbitMQ.

The tests in the example file publish an order, a price change and three paid orders, and check which queues each reached. The in-process RabbitMQ routes through the default, direct, topic, fanout and headers exchanges by the same bindings the descriptors declare. Testing a RabbitMQ service covers the harness.

This guide makes one service call another over RabbitMQ and wait for the answer. The orders service asks the inventory service whether an item is in stock before it accepts an order. The call goes over RabbitMQ's direct reply-to: no reply queue to declare, and no table of pending calls to keep by hand.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// The stock of one SKU. An RPC reply goes where the request asked, so the type names no /// destination. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] struct Stock { sku: String, available: bool, } #[subscriber("inventory.check", reply("inventory.check.unanswered"))] async fn check_stock(request: &CheckStock) -> Stock { tracing::info!(request.sku, request.quantity, "stock checked"); Stock { sku: request.sku.clone(), available: request.quantity <= 10, } } /// The inventory service's routes: each reply goes to the requester's own address. fn inventory() -> Router<LapinBroker, impl RouterDef<LapinBroker>> { Router::new() .include(check_stock) .out_reply(Publish::default()) .transform(DirectReplyTo) .build() } src/main.rs /// The stock of one SKU. An RPC reply goes where the request asked, so the type names no /// destination. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Stock { sku: String, available: bool, } struct Check; impl Handle<CheckStock, Stock> for Check { fn handle( &self, request: &CheckStock, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Stock, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(request.sku, request.quantity, "stock checked"); ready(Ok(Stock { sku: request.sku.clone(), available: request.quantity <= 10, })) } } /// The inventory service's routes: each reply goes to the requester's own address. fn inventory() -> Router<LapinBroker, impl RouterDef<LapinBroker>> { Router::new() .include( subscriber("inventory.check", Check) .reply() .to("inventory.check.unanswered") .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish::default()) .transform(DirectReplyTo) .build() } The inventory service answers with an ordinary handler that returns its reply. DirectReplyTo on the reply publisher sends each reply to the address the request named in its reply-to property, and copies the request's correlation-id onto it. Stock names no destination, because each reply goes where its request asked. The name in reply("inventory.check.unanswered") is where a request without a reply-to is answered, and what the service's AsyncAPI document reports. The routes are a Router, so the inventory service mounts them with b.include_router(inventory()) in its own app. The example runs both services in one process and mounts both routers.

RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include_router(orders()); b.include_router(inventory()); }) } src/main.rs /// How long an order waits for the inventory service. const RPC_TIMEOUT: Duration = Duration::from_secs(2); /// How long an order waits before it asks again when the inventory service did not answer. const RETRY: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Order { id: u64, sku: String, quantity: u32, } /// Asks the inventory service and waits for its answer. async fn ask_stock( inventory: &impl RequestReply, order: &Order, ) -> Result<Stock, Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> { let request = JsonCodec.encode(&CheckStock { sku: order.sku.clone(), quantity: order.quantity, })?; let reply = inventory .request( OutgoingMessage::new("inventory.check", request.as_ref()), RPC_TIMEOUT, ) .await?; Ok(JsonCodec.decode(reply.payload())?) } struct PlaceOrder; impl<Inventory> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Inventory,)>> for PlaceOrder where Inventory: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: RequestReply>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Inventory,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { match ask_stock(outs.get(DefaultSlot), order).await { Ok(stock) if stock.available => { tracing::info!(order.id, "order accepted"); Ok(()) } Ok(_) => { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order rejected, out of stock"); Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()) } Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(order.id, %err, "inventory unavailable, asking again later"); Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RETRY)) } } } } /// The orders service's routes: the requester is a policy, paired with the connection at startup. fn orders() -> Router<LapinBroker, impl RouterDef<LapinBroker>> { Router::new() .include(subscriber("orders", PlaceOrder).build()) .out(DefaultSlot, Request::default()) .build() } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); // The example runs both services in one process; each service mounts its own router. RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include_router(orders()); b.include_router(inventory()); }) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } place_order bounds its slot Out<impl RequestReply>, and the mount site pairs it with the Request policy, LapinRequest. Each request goes to the default exchange with the routing key inventory.check, so it reaches the queue of that name. It carries reply-to set to RabbitMQ's amq.rabbitmq.reply-to and a fresh correlation-id. The reply with the same id resolves the call; a reply with another id is dropped. The request and the reply are bytes here, so ask_stock encodes and decodes them with JsonCodec. RPC_TIMEOUT bounds the wait. When nobody answers in time, the call fails with AmqpError::RequestTimeout. place_order then asks for the order again in 30 seconds with retry_after, instead of guessing the stock. An item out of stock is a business answer, so the order is dropped. The policy takes the settings of a publish: exchange, priority and expiration. A request is transient by default: nobody waits for it after the timeout, so it gains nothing from surviving a restart. persistent(true) makes it persistent.

Direct reply-to is at-most-once. The reply address lives in the requester's channel on one RabbitMQ node, and nothing is queued durably. A reply in flight when that channel closes is lost, and the caller sees a timeout. The request itself is an ordinary message in an ordinary queue: when the inventory service is down, it waits in inventory.check and may be answered after the caller has given up. So the inventory call is safe to repeat: answering it twice changes nothing. The requester reads its replies on a channel of its own, opened by its first request.

Both sides speak plain AMQP 0.9.1. A responder written with another client consumes the request queue, publishes its reply to the default exchange with the routing key from reply-to, and copies the correlation-id. A RustStream responder with DirectReplyTo answers a requester written with another client the same way.

documents.t: An in-process RabbitMQ belongs to the app that connected it, so the requester and the responder must run in one app to talk. The tests start the example's app, which mounts both routers, and check that an order in stock is accepted and one out of stock is dropped. The third test mounts the orders router alone, with a paused clock: nobody answers, the request times out, and the order asks again later. The in-process RabbitMQ gives every request its own reply address and correlates the reply, as the server does. Testing a RabbitMQ service covers the harness.

A test runs the service's own app with TestApp, against an in-process RabbitMQ or against a running server. The service under test charges card payments. A payment arrives on the card-payments queue, and the handler replies with a receipt on card-receipts. A payment without an amount is dropped. A payment over the bank's instant limit is held: the handler asks for it again in a minute with retry_after. After three deliveries a payment goes to card-payments.review. The app is built by service(broker), so a test chooses the broker and main uses the production one. The tests need the testing feature of ruststream-lapin in [dev-dependencies].

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_payment_gets_a_receipt() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); let tb = TestApp::start(service(broker)).await?; a_receipt_follows_a_payment(tb).await } async fn a_receipt_follows_a_payment(tb: TestApp<()>) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { tb.broker::<LapinBroker>() .message(&Payment { id: 1, amount_cents: 2_500, }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<LapinBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.broker::<LapinBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("card-receipts") .assert_called_once() .with(&Receipt { payment: 1, amount_cents: 2_500, }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_payment_gets_a_receipt() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); let tb = TestApp::start(service(broker)).await?; a_receipt_follows_a_payment(tb).await } async fn a_receipt_follows_a_payment(tb: TestApp<()>) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { tb.broker::<LapinBroker>() .message(&Payment { id: 1, amount_cents: 2_500, }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<LapinBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.broker::<LapinBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("card-receipts") .assert_called_once() .with(&Receipt { payment: 1, amount_cents: 2_500, }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } TestApp::start connects LapinBroker to an in-process RabbitMQ. The URI is parsed as a connection would parse it, and never dialled. The test addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<LapinBroker>(). Payment declares its destination, card-payments, so the test publishes it with no to(..). publish returns once the handler and its reply have settled. So the next lines assert on finished state: how the subscriber settled and what reached card-receipts. The body takes the started app as an argument, so the live test below runs it too.

let tb = TestApp::start(service(broker)).await?; let held = Payment { id: 3, amount_cents: 250_000, }; tb.broker::<LapinBroker>().message(&held).publish().await?; tb.broker::<LapinBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(HOLD)); // The service holds the copy and publishes it back to the queue after `HOLD`. tb.advance(HOLD).await?; tb.broker::<LapinBroker>() .published::<Payment>("card-payments") .assert_called(2) .with(&held) .with_header(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER, "1"); // The third delivery is the last one: it goes to the review queue as it arrived. tb.advance(HOLD).await?; assert_eq!( tb.broker::<LapinBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .outcomes(), [Outcome::Nack, Outcome::Nack, Outcome::Nack], ); tb.broker::<LapinBroker>() .published::<Payment>("card-payments.review") .assert_called_once() .with(&held); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } src/main.rs #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)] async fn a_payment_the_bank_keeps_holding_goes_to_review() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); let tb = TestApp::start(service(broker)).await?; let held = Payment { id: 3, amount_cents: 250_000, }; tb.broker::<LapinBroker>().message(&held).publish().await?; tb.broker::<LapinBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(HOLD)); // The service holds the copy and publishes it back to the queue after `HOLD`. tb.advance(HOLD).await?; tb.broker::<LapinBroker>() .published::<Payment>("card-payments") .assert_called(2) .with(&held) .with_header(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER, "1"); // The third delivery is the last one: it goes to the review queue as it arrived. tb.advance(HOLD).await?; assert_eq!( tb.broker::<LapinBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .outcomes(), [Outcome::Nack, Outcome::Nack, Outcome::Nack], ); tb.broker::<LapinBroker>() .published::<Payment>("card-payments.review") .assert_called_once() .with(&held); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } The test starts on a paused clock, and advance moves it forward. A minute of HOLD costs nothing. The queue has no delay, so the service holds the copy and publishes it back to card-payments when the delay ends. The copy carries the retry count in a header, and published shows it next to the test's own message. The third delivery is the last one the mount site allows, so the payment goes to card-payments.review as it arrived. Each held delivery is recorded as Outcome::Nack.

documents.t: The in-process RabbitMQ reads the broker's settings and the descriptors of the routes, the same ones the server sees. declare_topology decides whether a subscription declares its queue, as on the server. It models RabbitMQ rather than a generic queue: The default, direct, topic, fanout and headers exchanges route by the bindings the descriptors declare. Competing consumers share a queue, and a requeue goes back through it. A queue keeps what reaches it while nobody consumes it, and a consumer that closes returns what it took and did not settle. A quorum queue counts deliveries and dead-letters a spent one through its route. A waiting queue releases a delayed copy, and direct reply-to gives every request an address of its own. A transaction stays invisible until it commits. It refuses what the server refuses: a name or a header the protocol cannot carry, a body over 16 MiB, a transient queue that is not exclusive, a binding on the default exchange, a queue declared again with other settings, a quorum queue with a priority. A delivery settled after its connection closed reports the closed channel. What only a server has needs one: the prefetch window, publisher confirms, the atomicity of a channel transaction, plugin exchanges, a queue two connections share, and a queue the service expects to find without declaring it.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn a_payment_gets_a_receipt_on_a_server() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let Some(url) = live::url("AMQP_TEST_URL") else { return Ok(()); }; let tb = TestApp::start_live(service(LapinBroker::new(url).declare_topology(true))).await?; a_receipt_follows_a_payment(tb).await } src/main.rs #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn a_payment_gets_a_receipt_on_a_server() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let Some(url) = live::url("AMQP_TEST_URL") else { return Ok(()); }; let tb = TestApp::start_live(service(LapinBroker::new(url).declare_topology(true))).await?; a_receipt_follows_a_payment(tb).await } TestApp::start_live connects the same app to a running RabbitMQ. The test reads the URI from AMQP_TEST_URL with live::url, a helper of the example's own, and skips when it is unset. The broker declares its topology, so the test runs on an empty server. The assertions are the in-process ones, unchanged. On a server, RabbitMQ picks which consumer of a queue takes a message, so a live test runs one subscription per queue. cargo test AMQP_TEST_URL=amqp://127.0.0.1:5672 cargo test -- --test-threads=1 The RabbitMQ of Getting started is enough for the live run.

documents.t: This guide describes a service's queues, exchanges and bindings, and decides who creates them: the service or the people who operate RabbitMQ. A queue descriptor states what the service expects to find on the server. Nothing is created unless the broker opts in with declare_topology(true). The example is a payments service with a replicated queue for payments, a queue for the payments that fail, and a queue of each instance's own for exchange rates.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] struct Payment { id: u64, card: String, amount_cents: u64, } /// Payments live in a replicated quorum queue; what it rejects goes to `payments.dead`. #[subscriber(RabbitQuorumQueue::new("payments").dead_letter_exchange("payments.dead"))] async fn charge(payment: &Payment) -> HandlerOutcome { if payment.card.is_empty() { tracing::warn!(payment.id, "payment without a card rejected"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::info!(payment.id, payment.amount_cents, "payment charged"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Every payment the `payments` queue dead-letters. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("payments.failed") .bind(RabbitExchange::fanout("payments.dead"), ""))] async fn record_failure(payment: &Payment) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::error!(payment.id, "payment failed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Payment { id: u64, card: String, amount_cents: u64, } struct Charge; impl Handle<Payment> for Charge { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if payment.card.is_empty() { tracing::warn!(payment.id, "payment without a card rejected"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::info!(payment.id, payment.amount_cents, "payment charged"); ready(Ok(())) } } struct RecordFailure; impl Handle<Payment> for RecordFailure { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::error!(payment.id, "payment failed"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// Payments live in a replicated quorum queue; what it rejects goes to `payments.dead`. fn payments_queue() -> RabbitQuorumQueue { RabbitQuorumQueue::new("payments").dead_letter_exchange("payments.dead") } /// Every payment the `payments` queue dead-letters. fn failed_queue() -> RabbitQueue { RabbitQueue::new("payments.failed").bind(RabbitExchange::fanout("payments.dead"), "") } RabbitMQ has two queue types, and the type is fixed when the queue is created. A classic queue lives on one node. A quorum queue is replicated over the cluster by Raft and survives the loss of a node. Each type has its own descriptor: RabbitQueue and RabbitQuorumQueue. Take a quorum queue for data that must not be lost, such as payments, and a classic queue for the rest. RabbitMQ's quorum queue guide compares the two. A quorum queue is always durable, shared between connections and permanent. So RabbitQuorumQueue has no durable, exclusive or auto_delete, and a quorum queue that contradicts its type does not compile. A quorum queue also counts the deliveries of each message, which the retries guide builds on. dead_letter_exchange gives payments a route for what it rejects. A payment charge drops goes to the payments.dead exchange, and from there to payments.failed, the queue bound to it. dead_letter_routing_key replaces the message's routing key on that route when the exchange routes by key.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] struct FxRate { currency: String, micros_per_euro: u64, } /// The name of this instance's own queue. fn rates_queue_name() -> String { format!("payments.rates.{}", process::id()) } /// A queue of this instance's own: it lives as long as the connection, and a rate older than a /// minute expires unread. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new(rates_queue_name()) .durable(false) .exclusive(true) .auto_delete(true) .argument("x-message-ttl", AMQPValue::LongLongInt(60_000)) .bind(RabbitExchange::fanout("fx-rates"), ""))] async fn update_rate(rate: &FxRate) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(rate.currency, rate.micros_per_euro, "exchange rate updated"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct FxRate { currency: String, micros_per_euro: u64, } /// The name of this instance's own queue. fn rates_queue_name() -> String { format!("payments.rates.{}", process::id()) } /// A queue of this instance's own: it lives as long as the connection, and a rate older than a /// minute expires unread. fn rates_queue() -> RabbitQueue { RabbitQueue::new(rates_queue_name()) .durable(false) .exclusive(true) .auto_delete(true) .argument("x-message-ttl", AMQPValue::LongLongInt(60_000)) .bind(RabbitExchange::fanout("fx-rates"), "") } struct UpdateRate; impl Handle<FxRate> for UpdateRate { fn handle( &self, rate: &FxRate, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(rate.currency, rate.micros_per_euro, "exchange rate updated"); ready(Ok(())) } } Every instance needs every exchange rate, so each instance reads a queue of its own, bound to the fx-rates fanout exchange. The queue name carries the process id, so two instances never share it. exclusive(true) lets only this connection use the queue, and RabbitMQ deletes it when the connection closes. auto_delete(true) deletes it once its last consumer is gone. durable(false) keeps it off the disk: rates are worthless after a restart. RabbitMQ 4 accepts a transient queue only when it is exclusive, so durable(false) comes with exclusive(true). argument passes a declaration argument the descriptor has no method for, here x-message-ttl: a rate nobody read within a minute expires. The same way sets x-max-length, x-max-priority, x-overflow or x-single-active-consumer. The value is an AMQPValue, and arguments takes a whole table.

Macros Manual src/main.rs fn service(broker: LapinBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(charge); b.include(record_failure); b.include(update_rate); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { // Development declares the topology; production runs with `DECLARE_TOPOLOGY=false` against // the queues operations created. let declare = env::var("DECLARE_TOPOLOGY").map_or(true, |value| value != "false"); service(LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(declare)) } src/main.rs fn service(broker: LapinBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber(payments_queue(), Charge).build()); b.include(subscriber(failed_queue(), RecordFailure).build()); b.include(subscriber(rates_queue(), UpdateRate).build()); }) } fn app() -> impl App { // Development declares the topology; production runs with `DECLARE_TOPOLOGY=false` against // the queues operations created. let declare = env::var("DECLARE_TOPOLOGY").map_or(true, |value| value != "false"); service(LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(declare)) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } With declare_topology(true), each subscription declares at startup what its descriptor states. It declares the exchanges its bindings name first, then the queue with its arguments, then the bindings. The default exchange and the built-in amq.* exchanges exist on every server and are never declared. A declaration repeats harmlessly while it matches what the server has, so every instance of the service declares the same queues. A declaration that differs from the existing queue fails. RabbitMQ answers PRECONDITION_FAILED to a queue declared again with another durability or other arguments, and the service does not start: AmqpError::Declare names the queue. A queue's type and arguments change by deleting and declaring it again, which loses what it holds, so they change through a migration, not a deploy. RabbitMQ explains which properties must match in property equivalence.

DECLARE_TOPOLOGY=false starts the same service with declaration off. The descriptors then declare nothing: they state the queues, arguments and bindings the service expects, and operations create them. A queue that does not exist fails the subscription at startup with AmqpError::Subscribe, so a missing queue stops the deploy instead of losing messages. Operations often set limits and TTLs with a RabbitMQ policy instead of declaration arguments. A policy changes a queue without declaring it again, and an argument set by a policy never conflicts with a service's declaration. The descriptor then names only what the service itself relies on. Declaration off also changes what a quorum queue's retry declaration can do, which the retries guide describes.

The tests in the example file reject a payment and find it in payments.failed, under declaration on and off. The in-process RabbitMQ follows the broker's setting: it declares what the descriptors state and refuses what the server refuses, such as a transient queue that is not exclusive, a binding on the default exchange or a queue declared again with other settings. With declaration off, every queue a subscription names is there in process, so a missing queue belongs to a live test. Testing a RabbitMQ service covers the harness.

This guide shares one RabbitMQ queue between the workers of a service and keeps the order where it matters. The example is an invoices service. Every instance reads the same invoices queue and renders what it takes. A second queue feeds an archive in batches, and a third feeds the ledger in strict queue order.

Every instance of the service subscribes to the same queue. RabbitMQ hands each message to one of them, in turn, and never to two at once. Starting another instance adds a consumer, and the queue drains faster. A message an instance took and did not settle goes back to the queue when its connection closes, and another instance takes it. The service needs nothing for this: the queue name in #[subscriber] is the same in every instance.

RabbitMQ sends a consumer nothing more while it holds that many. So a slow instance stops taking work, and the next message goes to an instance with room for it. Without a prefetch, RabbitMQ pushes the queue to its consumers as fast as the network allows, and a slow instance piles up messages the others could have taken. The count is a NonZeroU16: leaving it unset is how no limit is spelled. The broker's value applies to every subscription, and a queue descriptor overrides it for its own queue. The window is the server's, so a test sees it only against a running RabbitMQ.

Invoices with the same key go to the same lane, one after another, in the order the instance received them. Invoices of different customers run in parallel. An invoice without the header goes to the next lane in turn. RabbitMQ does not read the header: the lanes are the service's own convention. The order holds inside one instance. Two instances each take part of a customer's invoices, so their lanes do not order across instances. The handler reads Redelivered to log whether RabbitMQ delivered the invoice before.

The descriptor has no method for it, so argument passes x-single-active-consumer to the queue declaration as it is. The other instances stay subscribed and idle until they take over. The in-process RabbitMQ shares a queue between competing consumers and assembles batches as a server does. The prefetch window and single active consumer are the server's, so they belong to a live test. Testing a RabbitMQ service covers the harness.
